Lord Vexford is expected to ask formally for Elara's hand the day after his arrival; Elara will be presented in the gray gown and must endure the proposal, which will eventually become the announced engagement (the widower's hand) that tightens the trap around her.

Elara has begun planning the practical details of her escape — the key to the rear servant's door, the hour of the night watch, and the road to the sea — vowing she will not be bought. This plan will develop through the engagement and wedding chapters until she finally flees on the night before the wedding.

Kael told Elara that if he could choose his life fresh he would be a sailor with somebody on shore to light a fire for him when he came home — planting the seed of the cottage-by-the-sea dream that Elara will later voice as their shared hope of escape.

chapters.name: First Snow
chapters.content:
The first snow began before dawn, a sifting of small dry flakes out of a sky the color of a bruise, and by the time the house woke it had laid a thin white veil over the moors, softening every hard line of the world. Thornwood in snow was almost beautiful: the gray stone turned white, the iron fences wore a fur of frost, and the smoke from the kitchen chimneys rose straight and silver into the still air. The moors, which had been a gray sea all autumn, became a white one, and the horizon vanished into the falling flakes so that the estate seemed to float, cut off from everything, a ship becalmed in a silent harbor.

Elara stood at her window in her shift and watched it come down. She had lain awake most of the night, planning, and the snow felt like an answer of some kind, though she could not have said to what. The first snow of the year never lasted — it would melt by midday and the world would be mud again — but for a few hours the moors would be clean and blank, a page with nothing written on it yet, and there was a comfort in that she could not name.

The presentation was to happen after the morning meal, in the great hall. Margaret had decreed it; her father had not objected. Elara stood in her shift while Martha worked the pearl-silver gown up over her shoulders, and the girl in the glass looked modest and well-bred, exactly as a lord's daughter should look who was about to be dealt, and Elara smiled at her and the girl smiled back, a perfect mask.

The snow had stopped by then — brief, as she had known it would be — and the sun came out thin and white as she walked down the stairs. Vexford stood by the hearth in his black coat, warming his hands with the air of a man who was never cold anywhere for long. He turned when she entered, and his pale, colorless eyes took her in — the gray gown, the modest walk, the lowered gaze — and he smiled a thin, satisfied smile, like a man ticking a line off a list.

"Lady Elara," he said. "You look well this morning."

"My lord."

He crossed to her and took her hand, and this time he raised it to his lips and kissed it, dry and brief, and Margaret, watching from the stair, let out a small breath that might have been a sob of triumph. "A cold morning," he said. "But the moors are lovely in snow. Do you ride out today?"

"I thought I might, my lord. If the ground allows."

"Take care with the gray. The first snow makes the ground treacherous." He said it the way a man gives an order wrapped in courtesy, and Elara curtsied and said she would take care, and she saw her mother's face over his shoulder — bright, exultant, already measuring the width of a wedding veil.

But the formal words did not come. Vexford turned to her father and began, instead, to talk of the hunting — the birds he had marked on the eastern heath, the spaniels he had brought — and the two men fell into their circling talk of land and sport, and Margaret's smile tightened by a degree, and Elara understood, with a strange lightening of the chest, that he was not going to ask. Not yet. He was a man who dealt in his own time. Before he left, her father said later, when the talk had moved to the study and the door had closed behind them, he would have his answer.

Margaret was beside herself. "He kissed your hand," she whispered in the corridor, gripping Elara's wrist. "A man does not kiss the hand of a girl he means to let go. He will ask before he leaves. You must be perfect, Elara. Every day, perfect, until he asks. Go and be seen — walk in the garden, take the air, put some color in your cheeks."

Elara curtsied and went, and as soon as she was out of her mother's sight she did not go to the garden. She went to the stables.

The snow had begun again, a slower, heavier fall now, and the stable yard was white and quiet, the day's work done to a hush. No grooms about. The doors of the long stable stood open at the far end, and from within came the warm breath-smell of horses and hay and leather, and she stepped inside out of the falling flakes and stood a moment, letting her eyes adjust.

He was at the far end, at Storm's stall, with his back to her — a brush in his hand, moving in long, patient strokes down the gray gelding's shoulder. Storm had his head turned, lipping at the man's sleeve with the easy affection of a horse who knows the hand that feeds him, and Kael murmured something low, too low to hear, and the sound of it — the plain, unselfconscious tenderness of a man talking to a horse with no one to hear — stopped her in the doorway.

She had meant to say something. She had come with words prepared. But she stood and watched him a long moment, the brush moving, the snow drifting through the open door behind him and settling on the straw in a thin white line, and she felt the whole morning — the gray gown, the kissed hand, the mother's whispering, the cold-eyed man by the fire — lift off her shoulders and fall away.

He turned, and saw her, and the brush stilled in his hand.

"My lady."

"Don't." She heard her own voice, rougher than she meant. "Don't 'my lady' me. Not today."

He studied her a moment, level and unafraid, the way he looked at a horse that had come to him spooked. Then he set the brush down on the stall rail and said, quietly, "Bad morning?"

She came forward then, into the warm dim of the stable, and put her hand on Storm's neck. The gelding snorted and leaned into her palm. The snow whispered against the roof, soft and endless.

"He came to look at me," she said. "The lord from the south. He came to look at me the way a man looks at a horse he means to buy." She had not meant to say it so bald, so true. "My father says they shall deal. My mother had me dressed in the gray gown and walked me down like a prize mare to be shown."

Kael said nothing. He did not look away. He stood with his hand on the stall rail, very still, and let her speak.

"He kissed my hand," she said, and the words came out with a tremble she could not stop. "Today, in the hall, he kissed my hand, and my mother nearly wept with joy, and I stood there and smiled, and I thought — I thought of you. I stood there in that dress being priced, and all I could think of was you in the library, reading about the sea."

She stopped. The words hung in the warm air between them, and she had the terrible, freeing feeling of having said a thing she could not unsay, of having laid the coal from her heart down on the stall rail between them where he could see it burn.

He was quiet a long moment. The brush moved again, slowly, down Storm's shoulder — a steadying motion, and she understood that he was giving her time, the way he had given her time at the fence that day, time to recover her dignity before he came to her aid. When he spoke, his voice was low and rough, and careful, the way a man's voice is careful around a frightened animal.

"A man who looks at a person like a horse," he said, "is a man who has never once been looked at himself. Not truly. He doesn't know the difference."

"How do you know that?" she said.

"Because I've been the other thing." He turned to face her, brush in hand, his eyes steady and gray. "I've been a man with nothing, looked at like I was less than the dirt, and I've been looked at like I mattered. There's no mistaking the two. And that lord from the south — he'll never know what he missed, looking at you like you were a thing to be bought."

"Missed?"

"You're not a thing, my lady. That's all I know how to say it. You're not a thing to be bought and dealt." He said it simply, without daring, and she felt something break open in her chest, a dam of held-back terror and held-back everything, and she stood very still in the warm stable with the snow falling and let it break.

She did not cry. She had not cried since the mare died, and she did not cry now. But she stood with her hand on Storm's warm neck and let him see her face without the mask on it, and he looked at her the whole time, unafraid, and did not look away.

"They'll make me marry him," she said at last. "Before spring, I think. My father has decided. My mother has decided. It's already done in their heads — I heard them speak of the wedding, of Blackmoor Hall, as if I weren't in the room." She stopped. "I have to get out. I have to get out before it's too late."

He said nothing to that. He did not tell her it was impossible, did not remind her of her father's reach and the moors and the cold, though she knew he must be thinking it. He only stood and let the words stand, and after a moment he said, "When you go, you won't go alone."

She looked up at him sharply, and he met her eyes, and neither of them spoke of what he meant, and the snow came down past the open door and settled on the straw, and something passed between them in the warm dark of the stable that neither of them named.

He turned back to Storm, and she watched his hands move, patient and sure, and she thought of the dead mare and the grave under the hawthorn, and of the man who had told her he would want somebody on shore to light a fire for him, and she felt the coal in her chest settle and burn steady.

They did not speak much after that. The snow thickened, and the light through the door went gray and soft, and she helped him in a small way — held the halter while he checked Storm's hooves, handed him the curry comb when he asked — and it was the most companionable hour she had spent since the library, and it cost her nothing, and it gave her everything.

When the light began to fail, he walked her to the door. The yard beyond was white now, the thin first snow grown into a real fall, the moors vanished into the swirling flakes, and the cold came in sharp and clean past the warmth of the stable. She stood in the doorway a moment, the two of them close in the frame of it, the snow drifting past them into the dark, and she did not want to go. Up the yard, in the great house, her mother was already planning a wedding, and a man with colorless eyes was warming his hands at the fire, and all of it was waiting for her.

"I should go back," she said. "Before they notice."

"Aye."

She did not move. The snow settled on her shoulders, on the dark wool of the cloak Martha had laid out, and she looked at him in the failing light — the level eyes, the scarred hands, the mouth that had learned to smile over the word coast — and she wanted, with a fierceness that frightened her, to stay.

"Thank you," she said. "For listening. No one — " She stopped. "No one listens. In that house, no one hears a word I say. You're the only one."

"There's nothing to thank me for, my lady."

"It's not 'my lady' to you." The words came out before she could stop them, and she felt the blood come up into her face, and she could not look at him. "Not anymore. Not to you."

He was very still. She could feel him looking at her in the doorway, the snow falling between them, and she thought he might speak, and she did not know what she would do if he did. But he did not speak. He only reached past her, his hand closing on the doorframe to hold the door for her, and she turned to go — and her hand, brushing past his on the frame, touched it.

It was nothing. A brush of knuckles against the back of his hand, a fraction of a second, the accidental meeting of two hands on a wooden frame in the falling snow. Neither of them spoke. Neither of them drew away. Her hand lay against his on the cold wood for a moment that held the whole world in it, and then she stepped out into the snow, and the door swung closed between them, and she walked up the yard with her heart hammering and the touch still burning on her skin.

She did not look back. If she had, she would have seen him standing in the open door of the stable, his hand still on the frame where hers had been, watching her go.

She ate the evening meal with her mother and the men. Vexford was there again, courteous and cold, and he asked about the ride she had not taken, and she answered that the snow had turned her back, and he nodded and said a sensible girl knew when the ground was treacherous, and Margaret beamed as though he had paid her a compliment, and Elara smiled her mask-smile and thought of a warm, dark stable and a man's hand on a doorframe.

The snow did not let up. By the time Martha undressed her and banked the fire and left, it was a proper storm, filling the yard, covering the fences, blurring the moors into a single white silence, and Elara stood at the window in her shift and watched it come down and did not think of Vexford at all. She thought of his hands on Storm's shoulder, and the way he had said when you go, you won't go alone, and the touch on the doorframe, and she pressed her own hand to the cold glass and watched the snow and did not name the thing she felt, because some things, once named, become too heavy to carry, and she needed to carry this one a little longer.

In the loft above the tack room, Kael lay on his straw pallet in the dark, listening to the snow sift against the roof, the horses stamping warm in their stalls below. He had not lit a candle. He lay on his back with his hands behind his head and looked at the black shape of the rafters and thought about the doorway.

He could still feel it. The brush of her hand against his, the fraction of a second that had held the whole world in it, and the way she had stood in the snow-lit dark and said it's not my lady to you, not anymore, with the blood up in her face. He had lain in this loft for months telling himself a man in his place learned not to reach for what was not offered. Tonight the offering had been made, or nearly made, or had been there all along and he had only just now let himself see it — and he had not reached. He had let her go out into the snow.

He turned on his side, and the straw rustled, and below him the black gelding stamped once in its stall, and he thought of her walking up the yard through the falling snow to a house where a cold-eyed lord was being warmed at her father's fire, and he felt something move in his chest that was not hope — hope was a fragile thing, he had laid it down carefully — this was something heavier, something with roots, and it frightened him.

When you go, you won't go alone. He had meant it with his whole body, the way a man means a thing he has never once spoken aloud. And now the words were out in the world, and she had heard them, and she had touched his hand, and the snow was falling over all of Thornwood like a mercy, like a clean white page.

He lay in the dark and let the weight of it settle on him, and he did not name it either, and outside the loft the snow came down and covered the world in silence, and somewhere up the yard in the great stone house a girl pressed her hand to a cold window and held the touch of his hand against the glass, and the night closed over both of them, white and deep and secret, holding them, the way it would hold a secret for a long time to come.

set.name: Elara Ashworth
set.description: Lady Elara Ashworth, 19, dark-haired, sharp-eyed, angular jaw, restless hands; daughter of Lord Aldous and Lady Margaret Ashworth at Thornwood Estate, the first snow of winter has fallen. Was presented to Lord Vexford in the pearl-silver gray gown; he kissed her hand but did not formally ask, letting it be known he will ask before his fortnight's visit ends. Margaret ordered her to be 'perfect every day' until he asks. On the morning of the snow Elara slipped away from the presentation to the stables and found Kael brushing Storm; she confessed Vexford's appraisal, her mother's maneuvering, and that she must get out before it is too late. Kael listened without judgment and said 'When you go, you won't go alone.' She told him 'It's not my lady to you. Not anymore.' As she left she brushed her hand against his on the doorframe — a touch neither named, which she carried into the night. Continues planning her escape (the rear servant's door key, the hour of the night watch, the road to the sea); still wears the mask of compliance for her mother and Vexford, but hides nothing more from Kael about the trap. Thin, sleepless, pale; holds the thought of him like a coal against her heart.

set.name: Lady Margaret Ashworth
set.description: Elara's mother, 46, brittle, socially ambitious, rose-water scent. set.description: Sour-faced, efficient lady's maid, loyal to Lady Margaret; deft, impersonal hands; silent, careful. set.name: Lord Vexford

set.name: Kael
set.description: Stable hand and groundsman at Thornwood, mid-twenties drifter with no references; rough low voice, level gray eyes, quiet authority; sleeps in the loft above the tack room, eats in the kitchen. On the first snow he was brushing Storm when Elara came to him; she confessed her fear of the southern lord who is to buy her and her need to escape, and he listened without judgment, then said 'When you go, you won't go alone.' She told him it was not 'my lady' to him anymore; as she left, her hand brushed against his on the doorframe and neither drew away or spoke of it. He now knows the truth of the trap around her and that she means to flee, and he has pledged himself to her flight. His reading has grown certain; he still intends honest work and keeping his place through the winter, though the bond with Elara strains his proper station.

He kissed her hand and called her a sensible girl who knows when the ground is treacherous, but did not formally ask for her hand, letting it be known he would ask before his fortnight's visit ended. She confessed that Vexford appraised her like a horse, that her parents have decided on the marriage, and that she must get out before it is too late. Kael listened without judgment and said 'When you go, you won't go alone.' She told him it was not 'my lady' to him anymore; as she left, her hand brushed against his on the doorframe and neither drew away or spoke of what it meant. Both carried the touch into the dark, cold night; Elara now knows she will not flee alone, and Kael now knows the truth of her trap and her resolve.

chapters.name: The Unspoken Word
chapters.content:
Spring came to Thornwood the way all good things came to Thornwood: late, and quietly, and almost by accident. For weeks the thaw had been a rumor — a softening in the air, a drip from the eaves, a gray patch of bare ground appearing at the edge of the yard like a message pushed up out of the earth. Then one morning the east wind turned warm, and the last of the snow ran off the moors in a thousand bright threads, and the world that had been locked and white all winter stood up out of the mud and remembered it was green.

The first heather came up soft and brown-gold on the near slopes. The birds returned. The long, sullen house seemed to stretch itself, windows thrown open to the wet clean air, and even the stone felt less like a prison and more like a place where people lived. Elara stood at her bedchamber window on the first true spring morning with the sash up and the breeze on her face, and she breathed in the smell of turned earth and cold water and felt, for the first time in months, that she was not a creature being kept for market. She was a person in a world that had survived another winter.

The winter had been the longest of her life. Vexford's fortnight had lengthened into weeks, and the weeks had hardened into the whole locked season, because the snows had come down over the moors like a lid and closed every road south, and a man could not travel where the drifts stood taller than a horse. So he had stayed. He had stayed through the short gray days and the long nights, courteous and cold, playing cards with her father, walking the frozen yards in his black coat, looking at her across the supper table with those pale, colorless eyes that inventoried everything and warmed nothing. Margaret had spent the winter in a state of suspended triumph, certain each week that the question would come, and each week it had not, and she had taken to wearing her best gown to supper and counting the days aloud at breakfast like a woman keeping vigil at a shrine.

Elara had borne it all — the rehearsed curtsies, the small talk, the way her mother's hand found her arm and squeezed when Vexford so much as glanced her way — and she had borne it lightly, because she had had a place to go afterward. Every late afternoon, when the dinner hour was still an hour away and the house bent itself toward the kitchens, she slipped up the back stair, past the stillroom, to the cold north-facing room full of dust and dead air that no one else in Thornwood remembered was there.

He was always there before her. He had taken to coming early, she suspected, to sit in the servant's chair and wait, and the sight of him — the dark head bent over the rain-stained table, the scarred hands flat on a page — undid her a little more each day. The ritual had the shape of prayer: she pushed the heavy door ajar, and he looked up, and something in his face moved, and neither of them said what it was.

His reading had grown certain. The halting labor of the first lessons had smoothed into a sure, plain cadence, and the book of voyages had given way to other discards from the wet pile — a farmer's almanac, a battered volume of old ballads, a thick and crumbling history of the western ports. He read to her now as naturally as other men talked, and she listened, and the words passed between them like the words of a story told by firelight, and the room they had claimed for their own had come to feel, against all reason, like the warmest place in the house.

The change had happened sometime in the deep of winter, and neither of them had marked the hour. It was there in the way he had begun to save her the chair that caught the last of the light. It was there in the way she had begun to bring a candle stub from the kitchens, wrapped in her sleeve, and to light it without asking. It was there in the long silences that had once been full of effort and were now full of something else — a fullness, a charge, like the air before a storm, like the moment a held breath finally begins to strain against the walls of the chest.

They did not touch. That was the rule of it, though no one had spoken it aloud. The library was full of near-touches — a hand extended toward the same page and withdrawn, a sleeve brushing a sleeve as they turned, the candle passed from his palm to hers with fingers that did not quite meet. Each time, the space between them closed to a hairsbreadth and held, the way the air holds the note of a bell, and each time the moment passed, and the wanting went unnamed into the dark.

Spring made it harder. Spring loosened the house and loosened her, and the walks she took along the thawing lanes left color in her cheeks and a restlessness in her blood, and the library, which had been a refuge against the cold, became something else: a place where the air itself seemed to lean toward him.

On the afternoon it crested, the light through the north window had gone the particular gold of the hour before dusk. She had been reading to him — a page of the old history, the one about the harbor towns — and her voice had carried them both a long way from Thornwood, out to quays and masts and the salt smell of a world he had only ever seen on paper. She looked up from the page to ask him something, and found him staring at her.

Not looking. Staring. The book lay forgotten under his hand, and his face was stripped bare of every guard he owned — the wariness, the servant's deference, the careful levelness he wore the way other men wore coats. What was left was an ache so plain and so unguarded that it stopped her breath in her throat. It mirrored her own. It was the thing she had been carrying since the doorway in the snow, since the ford, since the dead mare's stall, and seeing it in his eyes — seeing her own hunger looking back at her — undid her as completely as if he had spoken it.

"Kael," she said. It came out barely a whisper.

He did not answer. He rose from the servant's chair, slow, the way a man rises when he has made a decision he is afraid of, and he took one step toward her, and then another, and the space that had been a hairsbreadth all winter began, at last, to close. She did not move. She could not have moved if the house had caught fire around them.

He reached for her. His hand came up — hesitant, scarred, trembling in a way she had never seen it tremble, not with the stallion, not with the dying mare — and it stopped an inch from her face, and hung there, and she watched him fight for the words he had been holding back for months.

"My lady," he said.

It was both things at once, she understood in that instant: a warning to himself, the last wall between him and the ruin of everything he had built here — the place, the winter, the hope — and a plea. A plea to her, that she not make him say it, that she not close the distance he could not cross, that she save him from himself.

She answered him. Not in words. She took the last step herself, and the inch between his hand and her face vanished, and she raised her own hand and pressed his to her cheek — his palm, cold and calloused and alive against her skin — and his breath came out of him in a sound that was almost a sob, and she felt the wall inside him give way.

He was going to kiss her. She knew it the way she knew her own heartbeat, and she wanted it the way she had never wanted anything, and she leaned up toward him, and the world narrowed to the space between their mouths, and —

The library door creaked.

They broke apart as if the sound had been a shot. She was on the far side of the table before she knew she had moved, and he was standing with his back to the shelves, his hands at his sides, his face smoothed into the servant's mask by an effort she could almost hear. The candle flame steadied. The dust settled. The creak hung in the air, and then resolved itself into footsteps — someone in the corridor beyond the heavy door, someone who had leaned against it or tried the handle, someone who had paused and then moved on, down the back stair, fading, gone.

Elara stood at the door with her hand flat on the wood, listening. The corridor was empty. The house was settling toward dinner, full of its usual distant sounds — a door closing, a voice calling, the clatter of the kitchen below — and no one came back. Whatever had brushed against the library door had been nothing: a passing maid, a draft, the old house shifting on its bones. It did not matter. The door had creaked, and the moment had broken, and the unspoken word lay on the floor between them like a dropped thing neither of them dared pick up.

He crossed to the table and gathered the book — the old history of the western ports — and set it carefully on the shelf where they kept the discards they had not finished. His hands were steady now. When he turned, he was the stable hand again, the groundsman, the servant who knew his place, and she hated it — hated that the mask had fallen back over the man who had looked at her with that ache — and she could not find it in herself to say a single true word.

"I'd best see to the horses," he said. "Before full dark."

"Kael." She said his name because she could not bear for him to leave with the mask on, and he stopped, and for a moment the man looked out at her from behind the servant's eyes. "It was only the door," she said. "No one came in."

"Aye," he said. And then, very quietly, with the door creak still between them: "It doesn't matter, my lady. It only has to happen once, and it's done. I won't be the ruin of you."

She opened her mouth to answer — to tell him that he was not her ruin, that he was the only true thing in her life, that the door could creak a hundred times and she would not care — but the words would not come, and he was already gone, soundless as a shadow, and the heavy door swung closed behind him with a soft click, and she was alone in the gold dusk with the candle burning and the book he had left behind and the word that still would not be spoken.

She stood a long time at the table. She put her hand flat on the page where his hand had been, the way she had done in the first weeks, and she pressed her palm to her own cheek where his hand had lain, and she closed her eyes and felt it still there — the ghost of his palm, the cold calloused warmth of it, the tremble.

In the loft above the tack room, Kael lay in the dark with his hands behind his head, and he could still feel it: her hand, small and warm, pressing his own to her face, and the way she had leaned up toward him, and the door, and the name he had given her — my lady — which he had meant as a wall and which had come out of him like a wound. He had almost crossed it. One inch. One inch and he would have been lost, and she with him, and the whole careful structure of the winter — the lessons, the candle, the swept corner of the dust — would have come down around them in the space of a kiss.

He had said he would not be the ruin of her. He lay in the dark and knew it for the lie it was. He had been her ruin from the moment he let her teach him the word coast. The only question left was how much of her he would take down with him when it ended.

Spring came in through the stable door, soft and warm and smelling of wet earth, and the horses stamped and blew in their stalls, and somewhere up the yard in the great house a girl lay awake with a palm pressed to her cheek, holding the ghost of a touch that had nearly crossed an inch and become everything.

Neither of them slept well that night. Neither of them named the thing that kept them awake. The word stayed where it had always been, unspoken, between them, waiting for a door that would not creak — waiting for the hunting lodge on the eastern edge of the moors, where the rain would come down and the walls would hold their secret, and the unspoken word would finally, at last, be said.

set.name: Elara Ashworth
set.description: Lady Elara Ashworth, now 20, dark-haired, sharp-eyed, angular jaw; restless hands. Spring has arrived at Thornwood; she walks the thawing lanes, color in her cheeks, the mask of compliance intact for her mother and Vexford. Her library lessons with Kael have become a fixed daily ritual through the winter into spring; his reading is certain now, and the space between them is charged with a longing neither names. One spring dusk he stared at her with an unguarded ache, rose and reached for her, and called her 'my lady' as both warning and plea; she answered by pressing his hand to her cheek, and he was about to kiss her when the library door creaked and they pulled apart. He left saying he would not be the ruin of her. She lay awake holding the ghost of his palm against her cheek; the unspoken word hangs between them. Still plans her escape (the rear servant's door key, the hour of the night watch, the road to the sea) and still knows she will not flee alone. Sleepless, thin, but alive with the secret; hides nothing of the trap from Kael.

Spent the whole winter in suspended triumph: Vexford's visit lengthened into the locked season and she expected the formal question each week, counting the days aloud at breakfast and wearing her best gown to supper. set.description: Sour-faced, efficient lady's maid, loyal to Lady Margaret; deft, impersonal hands; silent, careful. Dressed Elara through the winter and spring; saw nothing of the library, Kael, the near-kiss, or Elara's inner state. Remains unaware.

set.description: Titled nobleman, 48, widower, master of Blackmoor Hall in the south, courteous, cold, pale colorless eyes; looks at people and land as an inventory. His 'fortnight's' hunting visit lengthened into the entire winter when the snows closed the moors roads; he remained at Thornwood through the thaw, playing cards with Ashworth, walking the yards, appraising Elara at the supper table. set.description: Stable hand and groundsman at Thornwood, mid-twenties drifter, rough low voice, level gray eyes, scarred hands; sleeps in the loft above the tack room, eats in the kitchen. His reading is now certain; the library lessons with Elara are a fixed spring ritual. He left her with 'I won't be the ruin of you,' knowing it for a lie — he believes he has been her ruin since she taught him the word coast.
