She does NOT know Martha followed her to the lodge, delivered the secret to her father, or that Kael was seized on a false theft charge in the dead of night — her father's knowledge and his action remain invisible to her. Hidden flight funds intact (grandmother's pearl earrings, silver pin, coin in attic mattress seam). Location: Thornwood, asleep in her gray-silk bedchamber. Goal: flee with Kael on the night before the wedding. Condition: dangerously unaware that the blade has fallen and the world has already changed; she will wake to a house that has been altered while she slept.

set.name: Lady Margaret Ashworth
set.description: Elara's mother, brittle, socially ambitious, rose-water scent. Triumphant and relieved since Vexford asked: she calls Elara her June bride and is deep in the trousseau, the journey south, and guest lists for Blackmoor Hall. Slept dreamlessly through the night of Kael's seizure, unaware of everything — the affair, Martha's betrayal, her husband's orders, the seizure, or the dawn punishment to come. Location: Thornwood. Goal: see her daughter married to Vexford at midsummer. Condition: completely unaware.

set.name: Lord Aldous Ashworth
set.description: Elara's father, 54, tall, gaunt, gray-eyed, master of Thornwood, rules through silence and iron. Consented to the Vexford match; knows everything from Martha's report. This chapter he moved with surgical precision: no rage, no accusation of Elara. That evening, after supper, he gave Steward Hale his orders: at the third hour of the night take Bren and the new gate man, seize the stable hand Kael from the loft, bind him, produce the grandfather's silver chalice from the chapel, and charge him with theft. He confronted Kael privately in his study, threatened him with hanging at first light, and warned him that if he speaks Elara's name he will not be hanged quickly; Kael gave his silence. Ashworth then had Kael bound in the cellar storeroom beneath the north wing. He has decided the public punishment to announce at dawn will be flogging and banishment (not a hanging, which would invite outside inquiry); the hanging was the private threat used to break the man and ensure silence. He knows of the affair but not the specific flight plan or wedding-eve timing. Location: Thornwood. Goal: punish Kael publicly as a thief in a way that salvages the Vexford settlement and admits nothing about his daughter; dawn courtyard punishment comes next.

set.name: Martha
set.description: Sour-faced, efficient lady's maid, about thirty, deft impersonal hands, served Elara fifteen years. Her love for Kael curdled into venom after his refusal; she followed Elara to the lodge, witnessed the lovers through the shutters, and delivered the secret to Lord Ashworth in his study that afternoon, planting the thought that the lovers will run. This night she sat in her narrow room above the kitchen and listened to the sounds of the yard — the scuffle, the thud, the bolts — as Kael was seized, and felt the stone in her chest turn over like a key in a lock: satisfaction, named justice. She believes he is to be hanged (her own earlier assumption) and knows nothing of Ashworth's private threat or his true plan of flogging and banishment at dawn. She has told no one else. Location: Thornwood, her room above the kitchen. Goal: watch the blade fall at dawn and see Kael punished for choosing Elara over her.

set.name: Lord Vexford
set.description: Titled nobleman, 48, widower, master of Blackmoor Hall in the south, courteous, cold, pale colorless eyes. Formally betrothed to Elara; midsummer wedding set at Blackmoor Hall. Unaware of Kael, the affair, the oath, the planned flight, or the false theft charge and seizure. Location: Thornwood (preparing to leave south to ready Blackmoor Hall). Goal: the marriage and the settlement, undisturbed.

set.name: Kael
set.description: Stable hand and groundsman at Thornwood, mid-twenties drifter, rough low voice, level gray eyes, scarred hands. Seized from the loft above the tack room at the third hour of the night by Hale, Bren, and the new gate man; fought briefly, was bound, and was dragged to the study, where Lord Ashworth showed him the grandfather's silver chalice, accused him of theft, and told him he is to be hanged at first light — a false charge Kael knows to be false and understands is the price of touching what belonged to the lord. He understood in the study that Martha betrayed them and that Ashworth has known for a day. He gave his silence: he will not speak Elara's name, understanding that silence is the only gift left he can give her. Now bound by the wrists to the iron ring in the cellar storeroom beneath the north wing, feet just touching the earth, rope burning his wrists. His dark green hair ribbon from Elara remains tied on his wrist hidden under his sleeve — he curled his fingers toward it as far as the ropes allow, the one thing left that is his. His hidden savings in the knotted cloth under the loft floor were never retrieved and remain hidden there. He spent the dark hours thinking of the sea, the cottage that will never be built, and her face in the lamplight; he resolved that if there is any way to survive the dawn he will find it because she loved him. Does not know Elara remains asleep and unaware. Location: cellar storeroom, Thornwood. Goal: survive the dawn; never speak her name; keep her safe from the truth.

set.name: Steward Hale
set.description: Lord Ashworth's steward of twenty years, gray-faced, folded hands, the perfect tool of the house. This night he carried out the lord's orders: at the third hour he took Bren and the new gate man, seized Kael from the stable loft, bound him, produced the chapel's silver chalice, and delivered him to the study. He saw the falseness of the charge and the cost of it in Kael's face and decided, in the space of a breath, to be a tool rather than a man. He silenced Pip the stable boy with the threat that the boy could hang beside Kael. Location: Thornwood. Goal: serve Lord Ashworth; oversee the dawn punishment.

set.name: Pip
set.description: Young stable boy who sleeps in the stable loft, roughly a child in years; adores Kael, who has been good to him (Kael's kindness to the stable boy was noted by Martha). When Kael was seized in the night, Pip cried out that Kael never stole anything, and was lifted off the ladder by the new gate man and silenced with the threat that he could hang beside Kael. He now knows the accusation is false and has been warned to silence on pain of being turned off or worse. Terrified, grieving, powerless. Location: Thornwood stables. Goal: survive; may harbor a dangerous knowledge that no one will let him speak.

The evening after Martha's report, Lord Ashworth ate supper with his usual silence, showing nothing, then retired to his study and gave Steward Hale his orders: at the third hour of the night, take Bren and the new gate man, seize the stable hand Kael from the loft without letting him dress or speak, bind him, and bring him to the study with the grandfather's silver chalice from the chapel altar.

At the third hour of the night, Kael was seized from the loft above the tack room by Hale, Bren, and the new gate man; he fought briefly and was bound with rope that bit to the bone. In the study, Lord Ashworth produced the chapel's silver chalice, called him a thief, and told him he is to be hanged at first light, warning that if he speaks Elara's name he will not be hanged quickly. Kael understood Martha had betrayed them and that the lie was for the world, not for him; he gave his silence and was bound to the iron ring in the cellar storeroom beneath the north wing to await dawn.

When Kael was seized, the stable boy Pip cried out that Kael never stole anything and was lifted off the ladder by the new gate man, silenced with the threat that he could hang beside Kael, and warned by Hale to stay quiet or be turned off or worse. Pip now knows the accusation is false and is too terrified to speak.

Kael reached for the loose floorboard where his hidden savings (the knotted cloth of coin) lay beneath the loft floor, but was seized before he could recover it; the savings remain hidden under the loft floor at Thornwood, unrecovered, so the lovers' joint flight resources now consist only of Elara's hidden hoard (grandmother's pearl earrings, silver pin, coin in the attic mattress seam).

At first light, Kael will be cut down from the cellar storeroom and dragged into the courtyard, where Lord Ashworth will announce publicly that the punishment for theft is flogging and banishment (the hanging was only the private threat made to break him). Kael will be bound to the post while Elara, locked in her bedchamber by her mother's order, hears the first crack of the lash and counts every strike (chapter 17), before he is cut down and cast out onto the moors (chapter 18).

chapters.name: The Courtyard Dawn
chapters.content:
She woke to a light she did not recognize. It was the thin gray of the hour before full dawn, and for a moment Elara lay in her gray-silk bed watching it seep through the curtains, and she could not think why the light should frighten her. She had waked to gray mornings all her life. The moors were always gray.

And yet something in the quality of the light was wrong, the way a familiar room is wrong when one thing has been moved in it while you slept. She lay still and listened, and the house was not quiet the way a sleeping house is quiet. It was quiet the way a house is quiet when everyone in it is awake and trying not to be heard.

Then the sound came: boots on stone, many boots, crossing the yard below her window with a rhythm that did not belong to any morning she knew. And beneath the boots, carrying under them like water under ice, the murmur of voices, and the scrape of something heavy being set upright in the courtyard — a sound like a beam being stood on end, and then the dull brass note of a thing being hammered home.

Elara sat up. Her heart was already beating too fast, and she did not know why, and she hated that she did not know why because her body clearly knew something her mind would not yet admit.

She swung her legs out of bed and went to the door and set her hand on the handle, and the door did not move. She turned the handle fully and shoved, and the door did not move, and then she understood that this, too, had been arranged in the night, like everything else.

"Mama," she said, but it came out small, so she said it again, louder, with her fist against the wood. "Mama. Why is my door locked?"

For a long moment there was only silence, and then Lady Margaret's voice came through the panel, high and thin and wrong, like a shawl pulled too tight over something it could not cover. "It isn't locked, darling. It's just — fastened. For your own good. There is something you must not see."

"See?" Elara pressed her whole hand flat against the wood. "Mama, what is happening in the yard?"

"Nothing. A servant has been caught in a crime. Your father is — making an example of him. It is not for you." A pause, and then Margaret's voice frayed into something almost pleading. "A lady does not look at such things, Elara. A lady looks away. Go back to your bed. I will bring you tea myself."

Elara did not go back to her bed. She went to the window, because the window was the only door left to her, and she pulled the curtain back the width of her body and looked down into the courtyard, and the world stopped.

They had set the post in the middle of the yard, where the carts stood on fair days, the square oak post with its iron ring that she had seen all her life without ever once understanding what it was for. The household was gathered — the grooms and the maids and the kitchen girls and the men from the gate — standing in a loose ring with their faces turned away or down, and in the middle of that ring, between Steward Hale and Bren and the new man from the gate, stood Kael.

He was bare to the waist. She saw that first, the shocking pale expanse of his back in the gray light, the rope-burn stripes dark across his wrists where they had bound him in front of him now, his head up, his shoulders set. And even from the height of her window she could see the dark green ribbon tied to his left wrist, worn and limp, the only bright thing in the whole gray yard, and she pressed both hands to the cold glass and her breath came out of her in a sound she had never made before, a sound with no name in it.

No. No, no, no. Not him. Anyone but him.

Lord Ashworth stood at the head of the yard in his black coat with his hands clasped behind his back, and his voice carried up to her window the way his voice always carried — flat, unhurried, the voice of a man reading a sentence he had already signed.

"This man," he said, "was taken in the night with my grandfather's silver chalice in his keeping. A thief in this house is a rot in this house, and a rot is cut out whole." He let the pause lie on the yard. "The punishment for theft is flogging and banishment. He will be whipped at this post and cast out of Thornwood before the sun is fully up, and if he is ever seen on this land or near any member of this household again, he will be shot."

Kael said nothing. He did not look up at her window. That was the worst thing, worse even than the words: he did not look up. He stood with his head bowed a little, his bare back to the house, and she understood that he would not look up because looking up would give her away, and he would not do that, not even now, not even with his life coming apart in front of the whole yard. He would protect her with his silence to the very end. He had always meant to.

"Bren," said Lord Ashworth.

And Bren — the same Bren she had seen a hundred times, carrying coal, laughing at the kitchen door — stepped forward holding the lash, a long braided thing with a heavy knot at the end, and Elara heard herself make the sound again, the nameless sound, and she drove her fist against the glass.

No. No, don't. Don't touch him, don't—

She pulled at the window, but it was a casement that only opened inward, and the room was locked from the outside, and she could not reach him, could not go to him, could not do anything but stand in her gray-silk shift behind a pane of glass and watch the man she loved be made into a lesson.

The first crack of the lash came like a shot fired inside her own chest.

It was louder than she had imagined, a wet, flat crack that seemed to go into the stone of the house and up through the floor into her bones, and she saw Kael's whole body arch against the post, his spine bowing, his bound hands clenching, and she saw the red line open across his shoulders like a mouth.

And he did not scream.

That was what broke her. Not the blow — she had braced for the blow, some part of her had been waiting for it since the moment she saw the post — but the silence after it. The yard was silent, the maids had their hands over their mouths, the grooms stared at their boots, and Kael hung against the post with his teeth set and made no sound at all, because he would not give them his voice, would not let them have even that.

"One," Elara whispered, and she did not know she was counting, could not have stopped herself if she had known. She pressed her hands flat against the cold stone of the wall beside the window — the wall her father's house was built of, the wall that had held her all her life, and now held her away from him — and she pressed so hard the grain of the stone bit into her palms.

The second crack came, higher, across the shoulder blades, and Kael's hands went white-knuckled where they gripped the ring of the post, and the red line crossed the first like a lattice, and still he made no sound.

"Two," she said. And then, because the sound of his silence was worse than any scream could have been, because a scream would have meant he was still fighting, would have meant he was still hers, still reaching for her across the distance — she began to count aloud, steadily, the way she had counted the days to the wedding, the way she had counted the days to the flight, as if by naming each blow she could take it onto herself. As if she could stand in the yard in his place.

Three. The lash came down across his ribs and she felt it in her own side, a stitch of phantom pain, and she pushed her forehead against the cold glass and thought: that one is mine. Four. She counted the strokes and she flinched with each one, and somewhere in the middle of it, between seven and eight, the counting became something else — a fever, a chant, a way of refusing the fact that it was his back and not hers. She pressed her palms to the stone and imagined every wound on her own skin, willed it, begged whatever god or chance ruled such things to let the next blow fall on her and spare him, and the blows kept falling, and she kept counting, and he kept not screaming.

Ten. His back was a ruin of red and purple lines, the skin split in half a dozen places, blood running thin and dark down his sides to soak the waistband of his trousers, and his legs had begun to tremble under him, the way a horse's legs tremble when it has run itself past sense. But his head was still up. His jaw was set. He had not made a sound.

Eleven. She saw his knees buckle, saw him catch himself against the iron ring and hang there for a heartbeat with his weight on his bound arms, and she thought, that one was for the cottage, and twelve, that one is for the door that stays, and thirteen, that one is for the sea he will never see, and she was weeping now, tears running down her face onto her shift, and she did not feel them, could not feel anything except the counting and the stone and the impossible, unbearable dignity of his silence.

Fourteen. She heard Margaret's voice somewhere behind the door, high and frantic, "It's over now, it's over, come away from the window, darling, come away—" and she heard it the way she heard the wind, without sense, and she did not move. She could not move. Her hands were nailed to the stone.

Fifteen. The lash fell and Kael's body went slack, and she saw Hale step forward and catch him by the arm before he could fall, and she saw Bren lower the lash, breathing hard, and she understood that it was over, that fifteen was the number, that they had counted the strokes for him the way she had counted them for him, and that he had survived them, and that was the only mercy in the whole gray morning.

She let go of the stone. Her palms were scored with the pattern of the wall, a dozen small red crescents where the grain had bitten her, and she looked at them, and then she looked down into the yard, and she saw them cut Kael down from the post.

He could not stand. That was the thing she would remember for the rest of her life, the thing that would come to her in the dark for years: not the sound of the lash, but the way he could not stand, the way Hale and Bren had to hold him up between them while he found his feet, the way he stood there swaying with his back a ruin and his head down and his hands shaking, and still — still — he did not look up at her window, because looking up would have been a confession, and he would not confess her to the whole yard.

They threw a shirt at his chest without helping him into it, and a pair of boots, and a crust of bread that fell in the mud and stayed there, and Ashworth's voice came again from the head of the yard, unhurried and final: "The east gate. If you are seen on this land again, you are a dead man. That is the whole of the law I keep."

Kael stood for a moment with his back to the house, and Elara saw his shoulders move as he dragged the shirt over his ruined skin — saw him flinch, saw him set his jaw and finish, slow and deliberate, pulling the collar straight as if it mattered, as if he were still the man who mended fences with level gray eyes and never hurried — and then he walked toward the east gate, barefoot now, because he had not put on the boots, and his gait was crooked and wrong and he did not look back.

She watched him go. He crossed the yard like a man crossing water, and the household stood silent and parted for him like a sea, and the east gate was dragged open, and he went through it, and the gate was dragged shut behind him, and the bolts were shot, and he was gone — out onto the moors, into the gray, with his back bleeding through his shirt and no coat and no horse and no food, and the whole of the world's cruelty still ahead of him, and he had not once made a sound.

Elara stood at the window until he had disappeared into the mist that swallowed the eastern field, until there was nothing left of him but the memory of a dark green ribbon and a man who would not scream, and then she slid down the wall until she was sitting on the cold floor with her back against the stone, and she held her scored palms up to the gray light and looked at them, and she pressed the heels of her hands into her eyes.

Behind the door, Margaret's voice was still going, high and soothing and utterly meaningless: "It's over now. It's over. See, it's quite over, darling. A little longer and we'll have your tea, and then the seamstress, and then—"

Elara lowered her hands. Her face was wet and her chest was hollow in a way she had never known a chest could be hollow, but her voice, when it came, was flat and clear, a stranger's voice, the voice of the person she was becoming in the space of that gray dawn.

"Go away, Mama."

"Elara—"

"There was no chalice. You know there was no chalice." She said it evenly, without heat, the way her father said things, and she heard Margaret's breath catch on the other side of the door, and she did not care. "He never stole anything in his life. He was the only honest man in this house. And you locked me in to watch them whip him." She turned her face to the window, where the mist had already closed over the eastern field like water over a stone. "I counted every stroke. Fifteen. And he never made a sound, Mama. Not one. That is what you did. You broke nothing but yourself."

The silence on the other side of the door went on a long time, and then there was the rustle of Margaret's skirts retreating down the hall, and the sound of the key turning in a lock that did not matter anymore, because Elara had already stopped being the kind of woman who waited for doors to open.

She got up from the floor. She went to the window and stood there with her hands flat against the cold pane, looking out at the moors where he had gone, and she did not weep. She did not call for Martha, and she did not ring for tea, and she did not lie down in her gray-silk bed.

She stood at the glass and she counted again, the way she had counted the days to the wedding, the way she had counted the strokes of the lash — only now she was counting something else, something that had begun in her chest in the moment she saw the post, something that was still growing, still hardening, still setting like a thing left out overnight in the frost. She counted the days until midsummer, and then she counted the nights, and then she stopped counting, because she had reached a number better than any number in the world.

She did not say it aloud. But she stood at her window in the gray dawn with the imprint of the stone wall scored into her palms, and she made the plan she had always been making, only now it was not a plan. Now it was a sentence.

The mist took the moors. The house settled back into its silence. And in the courtyard below, the servants came out with water and sand to wash the yard, and the red washed away, and the oak post stood empty in the middle of the morning light, and no one said the stable hand's name, but everyone knew the lady of the house had been watching from her window, and everyone knew the lady of the house had gone quiet in a way that had nothing of grief in it.

And in her bedchamber, Elara Ashworth stood at the glass until the day was fully up, and then she turned from the window and began, very carefully, to prepare for war.

set.name: Elara Ashworth
set.description: Lady Elara Ashworth, now 20, dark-haired, sharp-eyed. Woke at dawn to find her bedchamber door locked by her mother's order and watched from her window as Kael was bound to the post in the courtyard, bare to the waist, and flogged fifteen strokes for a theft she knows he did not commit (she saw the dark green ribbon on his wrist, the only bright thing in the yard). She pressed her hands flat against the cold stone beside the window so hard the grain scored her palms with small red crescents, counted every stroke aloud (one through fifteen), imagined each wound on her own skin, and was broken more by his endured silence than by any scream — he never made a sound, never looked up at her window (to protect her). She watched them cut him down, throw a shirt at him, drag open the east gate, and banish him barefoot onto the moors until the mist swallowed him. She told Lady Margaret through the locked door, flat and clear: 'There was no chalice... I counted every stroke. Fifteen. And he never made a sound.' She has stopped weeping; grief has hardened into cold resolve. She now knows her father knows (or at least acted on knowledge), knows Martha's betrayal is likely, and knows the house will lie about him. She no longer waits for doors to open — she will prepare for war (chapter 20 onward), counting the days to midsummer and the flight. Hidden flight funds intact (grandmother's pearl earrings, silver pin, coin in attic mattress seam). Location: Thornwood, her gray-silk bedchamber at the window. Goal: flee with Kael before the wedding, now driven by fury and grief; find him on the moors. Condition: transformed — no longer unaware, no longer a prisoner waiting; the blade has fallen and she has seen it fall.

set.name: Lady Margaret Ashworth
set.description: Elara's mother, brittle, socially ambitious, rose-water scent. At dawn she had Elara's bedchamber door fastened by her own order and stood outside it telling her daughter it was 'not for her' to watch a servant being made an example of. She heard, through the locked door, Elara's flat accusation ('There was no chalice... I counted every stroke') and retreated down the hall in silence, shaken — she now knows (or strongly suspects) Elara knew the man and that the theft charge was false, and that her daughter has gone quiet in a way that is not grief. She will bury this knowledge and accelerate the trousseau and wedding preparations, telling herself a wedding will cure it. Location: Thornwood. Goal: see her daughter married to Vexford at midsummer, keep up appearances. Condition: shaken, aware her daughter knows something, determined to look away.

set.name: Lord Aldous Ashworth
set.description: Elara's father, 54, tall, gaunt, gray-eyed, master of Thornwood. At dawn, in the courtyard before the gathered household, he announced the false charge and the sentence: 'The punishment for theft is flogging and banishment,' fifteen strokes at the post, then cast out of Thornwood, with the warning that if Kael is ever seen on the land or near any member of the household again he will be shot. He stood at the head of the yard in his black coat and watched Bren lay on all fifteen strokes, then had Kael cut down and thrown out the east gate. He believes the matter is closed and the Vexford settlement salvaged; he does not know Elara watched the whole flogging from her window or that her resolve has hardened into active war preparation. Location: Thornwood. Goal: keep the settlement intact, the house unashamed, and his daughter married at midsummer. Condition: satisfied that the rot has been cut out cleanly; unaware of the fury he has seeded in his daughter.

set.name: Martha
set.description: Sour-faced, efficient lady's maid, about thirty, deft impersonal hands, served Elara fifteen years. At dawn she watched the courtyard punishment she helped arrange: Kael flogged fifteen strokes and cast out the east gate. She believes her betrayal has landed exactly as intended — but she also saw Elara at the window through the morning light and saw how the lady watched and went quiet; a thread of unease now runs under her satisfaction, because a quiet lady is a lady she cannot read. She knows the full truth (the affair, her own report to Ashworth, the false charge) and has told no one else. She will now watch Elara's 'recovery' with the same cold vigilance as before, telling herself the danger is over. Location: Thornwood. Goal: see Kael punished (done) and the household return to order; keep her place and her secret. Condition: satisfied, watchful, faintly uneasy.

set.name: Lord Vexford
set.description: Titled nobleman, 48, widower, master of Blackmoor Hall, courteous, cold, pale colorless eyes. Formally betrothed to Elara; midsummer wedding set at Blackmoor Hall. He was not present in the yard at dawn (the flogging was household business) and remains unaware of Kael, the affair, the false theft charge, or the punishment. Location: Thornwood (preparing to leave south to ready Blackmoor Hall). Goal: the marriage and the settlement, undisturbed.

set.name: Kael
set.description: Stable hand and groundsman at Thornwood, mid-twenties drifter, rough low voice, level gray eyes, scarred hands. At dawn he was dragged from the cellar storeroom into the courtyard, stripped to the waist, and bound to the oak post by his wrists (the iron ring). Lord Ashworth publicly announced the false theft charge and the sentence of flogging and banishment. Bren laid fifteen strokes with the braided lash; Kael's back is now a ruin of split skin and red lattice lines, bleeding through the shirt that was thrown at him. He did not scream, did not cry out once, and never looked up at Elara's window — protecting her to the last. His knees buckled at the end; Hale caught him before he fell. He was cut down, given a shirt (which he dragged over his ruined back, flinching, setting the collar straight with deliberate calm) and boots he left behind, and a crust of bread that fell in the mud. He walked barefoot through the parted household to the east gate and out onto the moors, where the mist swallowed him, with no coat, no horse, no food, and no destination but the sea. His dark green ribbon from Elara remains tied on his wrist hidden under his sleeve. His hidden savings in the knotted cloth under the loft floor were never retrieved and remain hidden at Thornwood. He does not know Elara watched, counted every stroke, or has vowed to find him. Location: the open moors east of Thornwood, wounded, walking barefoot toward the sea. Goal: survive the moors, reach the coast, never speak her name; keep her safe from the truth. Condition: badly flogged, bleeding, in shock, alone on the moors.

set.name: Steward Hale
set.description: Lord Ashworth's steward of twenty years, gray-faced, folded hands. At dawn he oversaw the courtyard punishment: he held Kael's arm when the man's knees buckled after the fifteenth stroke, then oversaw the cutting down and the casting out through the east gate. He watched the lady's window once and saw her standing there, and has decided to forget he saw it. Location: Thornwood. Goal: serve Lord Ashworth; maintain order. Condition: a tool who has chosen to remain a tool.

set.name: Pip
set.description: Young stable boy who sleeps in the stable loft, roughly a child in years; adores Kael. He was silenced the night before with the threat that he could hang beside Kael, and at dawn he stood at the back of the gathered servants and watched his only friend flogged and cast out. He is now grieving and terrified, holding the dangerous knowledge that the accusation was false, knowing no one will let him speak. Location: Thornwood stables. Goal: survive; quietly mourn. Condition: broken-hearted, silenced, powerless.

At dawn in the courtyard, Lord Ashworth publicly announced the false theft charge and sentenced Kael to flogging and banishment. Kael was bound bare to the waist to the oak post and Bren laid fifteen strokes with the braided lash; Kael never made a sound and never looked up at Elara's window. He was cut down (Hale caught him when his knees buckled), given a shirt he dragged over his ruined back and boots he left behind, and cast out barefoot through the east gate onto the moors with no coat, horse, or food. This completes the dawn punishment and begins the banishment (chapter 18) and Elara's hollow days (chapter 19).

Lady Margaret had Elara's bedchamber door fastened at dawn by her own order. Elara watched the entire flogging from her window, pressed her hands against the cold stone until the grain scored her palms with red crescents, counted all fifteen strokes aloud, and was broken more by Kael's endured silence than by any scream. Through the locked door she told Margaret flatly that there was no chalice and that she counted every stroke; Margaret retreated shaken. Elara's grief hardened into cold resolve to prepare for war and find Kael, ending the chapter with her turning from the window to plan.

After witnessing Kael's flogging and banishment, Elara's resolve hardens: in the coming weeks (chapters 19-22) she will endure the hollow days, then begin eating and moving about the house again while secretly studying her father's schedule, the locks, and the moor paths, and accepting Bess's aid, so that she can flee on the night before the wedding (chapter 23).

Kael, flogged and cast out barefoot with no coat, horse, or food, must survive the moors and reach the eastern coast, where he will live rough in a fishing village (chapters 24-25), so that Elara can find him there after her flight.

Pip the stable boy witnessed Kael's seizure, knows the theft charge was false, and was threatened with hanging to silence him; he watched the flogging. His dangerous knowledge may surface later or remain buried; he now hates Martha and fears the house.

chapters.name: Cast Out
chapters.content:
He could not feel his back. That was the first strange thing — that a man could be cut down from a post with his skin in ribbons and feel nothing at all but a vast, spreading cold, as if the lash had flayed not flesh but some outer layer of himself that had been keeping him warm, and what was left of him now stood shivering at the center of his own body, watching the rest from a great distance.

The yard tilted. Hale's hand was still clamped on his arm, and Bren had taken the other, and between them they held him upright while the blood ran down his sides and soaked into the waistband of his trousers and made dark runnels down his legs. The stones of the yard were cold under his bare feet. He was aware of that with a strange, detached clarity: the cold of the stones, the way the household stood in a loose ring watching him the way people watch a thing that has been finished, the way the morning light had gone from gray to a paler, harder gray, the way the mist was already creeping in from the east field like something with a purpose.

They threw a shirt at his chest. It hit him and he caught it against his stomach without thinking, and he stood there with the folded cloth in his hands and felt the whole yard watching to see what he would do.

He dragged it over his head. The cloth touched his back and the cold disappeared, and what replaced it was a white wall of pain that went up his spine and into his skull and knocked the breath out of him through his teeth, and he heard himself make a sound — a short, ragged sound, the first sound he had made since they took him from the loft — and he hated it, hated that they had gotten that out of him too, and he stood there with his jaw set until the wall of white receded to a red roar, and then he set the collar straight, slow and deliberate, the way a man sets a collar when it matters, and he did it because it was the only thing left to him that he could do with dignity.

The boots lay in the mud where they had thrown them. He looked at them, and he did not stoop for them. He did not know why, exactly — some part of him knew that a man walking barefoot into the moors with his back opened to the bone would not get far, and that the boots were the only mercy the morning had offered, and that he was a fool to leave them — but there was something in him that would not bend to pick up what they had thrown at his feet, would not take the crust of bread lying in the mud beside them, would not let them have the sight of his hunger and his need. It was a small, stupid defiance, and he knew it, and he walked past the boots anyway.

"Kael."

The voice was low and close. Hale. Kael stopped, and turned his head a little, and Hale stood at his elbow with his gray face and his folded hands, and for a moment the steward's mouth worked as if he meant to say something, and then it closed, and he said only, "The east gate."

Kael looked at him. He looked at the man who had held him up at the post, who had caught him when his knees buckled, who had overseen the binding and the walking and the rest of it, and he found he had nothing in him for Hale, not even anger. Hale was a tool. Tools did what they were made to do. Kael had been a tool himself in a hundred yards and a hundred houses, and he knew the shape of a man who had chosen to be a tool until it was too late to be anything else.

"The east gate," Kael repeated. His voice came out cracked and dry, and he cleared his throat and tried again, and it came out no better. "And the warning. I heard it. Seen on the land, shot on sight. Near the lady—" He stopped. He had not meant to say the word. The word was a trap, and he knew it, and he could feel the whole yard lean in to catch what he would say next, could feel Ashworth's flat gaze on him from the head of the yard like a weight.

He did not finish the sentence. He turned, and he walked toward the east gate.

Walking was harder than standing. Each step sent a new wave through his back, and the shirt clung to the wounds and pulled at them with every breath, and by the time he had crossed half the yard he was walking crooked, listing, and he could feel the blood working its way down the backs of his legs. The household parted for him the way water parts around a stone, and he did not look at any of them. He did not look for Pip among the grooms, though some part of him knew the boy would be there, would be watching, would be carrying the same impossible knowledge he was carrying. He did not look up at the house.

He did not look up at the window.

There was a window above the courtyard, on the second floor, gray-silk curtains, and he had known, from the moment they bound him to the post, that she would be behind it. He had not looked at it once. He had kept his eyes on the stones, on the ring of the post, on the gray sky, on anything in the world except the one window where the whole of his ruin had its cause and its meaning — because if he had looked up, they would have seen. The whole yard would have seen, and Ashworth would have had his proof, and the lie he had built with his silence would have come apart, and she would have been left with nothing at all to protect her.

So he did not look. He crossed the yard with his eyes on the east gate, and he heard the sound of his own bare feet on the stones, and he felt the cold of the morning on his wet skin, and he thought, in the flat distance of his shock, that at least she would not have to watch him fall.

The east gate was a tall oak thing banded with iron, and it stood open before him, and beyond it the drive gave way to the east pasture, and beyond the pasture the moors began — a gray sea of heather and mist that swallowed the horizon, that had no fences and no walls and no end, that had been the whole world to him for a season and was now the whole world again, only worse, because he was leaving the only place in it that had ever held anything for him.

He stopped in the mouth of the gate.

Behind him, the yard was silent. He could feel them all there, watching, waiting for him to be gone so the morning could resume its ordinary shape. He could feel Ashworth's gaze on his back. He could feel the mist curling in from the moors, cold and damp, and he could feel, faintly, high up and far away, the prickling awareness of the window he had not looked at, would not look at, would not give them the gift of looking at.

He took a breath. It hurt. Everything hurt, and the hurt was a kind of anchor, the only thing that felt real in the whole unreal morning, and he held onto it the way a man holds onto a rope.

Then he stepped through the gate, and he did not look back.

The mist closed around him almost at once. It was thicker than it had looked from the yard, a damp gray that swallowed the house behind him and the trees and the fence line and, within a dozen steps, even the gate itself, so that he was walking in a world made only of gray and the sound of his own ragged breathing and the wet crunch of heather under his bare feet. He walked. He did not know where he was going — east, that was the direction of the gate, and east was as good as any, because the sea was somewhere east and the sea was the only destination his twenty years of wandering had ever left him with — and he walked, and the cold spread up from his feet and down from his shoulders and met somewhere in the middle of him, and the pain in his back settled into a steady red rhythm that kept time with his heartbeat.

He did not get far before his knees gave out.

It happened without warning: one step the world was upright and the next it was tilting, and he put his hands out and caught himself on a tussock of wet grass and lay there on his hands and knees in the mist, breathing in the smell of wet earth and heather, his back on fire, his arms shaking. The ground was cold and good against his palms. He stayed there a long time, and the mist moved around him, and he listened to the sound of his own breathing and the small sounds of the moor — the drip of water, the distant call of a curlew, the wind moving through the heather like a hand through hair — and he thought about nothing at all, because thinking was a luxury his body could not afford.

He got up. He did not know how long he had lain there — minutes, maybe, or longer — and he got up the way a horse gets up, all at once, and stood swaying in the mist with his hands on his knees until the world steadied, and then he walked on.

The ribbon was still on his wrist.

He noticed it when he put his hand down to steady himself against a wall of rock that loomed out of the mist — a long shoulder of granite that he had to climb around, and he put his hand out and felt the dark green cloth against his skin, damp and soft, and he stopped and looked at it. It was worn and limp, stained with his blood now where the rope had bitten, but it was still there, still tied, still the only bright thing in the whole gray world.

He touched it. He stood in the mist on the shoulder of the rock with his back on fire and his feet bleeding and his whole body one long ache, and he touched the ribbon, and for a moment something in his chest cracked open, the way a thing cracks when it has been held too tight for too long, and he stood there with his hand over the ribbon and his eyes closed and let it happen, because there was no one to see, no one to take it from him, no one in the whole gray world to know that the stable hand had stopped on the moors to hold the lady's ribbon against his wrist.

He did not say her name. He had promised himself, in the cellar in the dark, that he would never say her name again, that the only gift he had left to give her was the gift of his absence, that as long as he was alive and far from Thornwood, the lie held, and she was safe. He did not say her name. But he stood there in the mist with his hand over the ribbon until the shaking passed, and then he walked on.

The mist thinned as the morning wore on, and the moors opened out around him in their endless gray folds, and he walked because there was nothing else to do. He followed the lie of the land east, where the ground fell toward the low country, and he drank from a stream that ran cold and brown over stones, and he did not eat because there was nothing to eat, and his back bled through the shirt in patches and then stopped, and the pain settled from a roar into a deep, grinding ache that he carried the way he had carried every ache of his twenty-odd years, one step at a time.

Sometime in the afternoon the mist burned off and the sky showed a pale, watery sun, and he found himself on a rise of ground above a shallow valley, and he stopped, because from here he could look back the way he had come.

He had not meant to look back. He had promised himself he would not look back. But the rise gave him the whole of the eastern moors at his back and, beyond the shoulder of the land, a long gray smudge on the horizon that was, impossibly, the roof of the house he had walked out of that morning — Thornwood, small and gray and far away, with a curl of smoke standing straight up in the still air, and beyond it nothing but the endless moors.

He stood there a long time. He stood there until his legs began to shake again, and he watched the smoke of the house where she was, where she would always be, where they would dress her in gray silk and walk her down an aisle and give her to the cold-eyed man, and where he could never go again, not for any reason, not even to die on the doorstep.

He did not say her name. He stood on the rise in the pale afternoon light with the wind moving over the heather, and he touched the ribbon on his wrist, and then he turned his back on the house and he walked east, toward the sea he had never seen, and he did not look back again.

Behind him, Thornwood lay in its silence. The servants had washed the yard by noon, and the red was gone from the stones, and the oak post stood empty in the middle of the light, and no one said the stable hand's name, and everyone understood that the name had become a thing that must not be spoken, like a debt, like a grave.

In her bedchamber, Elara stood at the window until the mist had swallowed him, and then she stood there long after, until the mist thinned and the moors opened out empty and gray and there was no figure in them anywhere, no man walking barefoot, no dark green ribbon, nothing at all but the heather and the wind. She stood with her hands flat against the cold glass, the scored crescents in her palms white against the pane, and she watched the place where he had been until the light itself began to fail.

Margaret came to the door at noon with tea on a tray and the seamstress's note, and Elara did not answer. Martha came at dusk to draw the curtains, and found her standing in the dark at the window, and made to speak, and then did not, and went away again. The house settled into its evening with the door still fastened, and no one dared to unfasten it, and the silence that settled over Thornwood was a new silence, a silence with a shape to it, like the silence that follows a death.

Elara watched the dark come down over the moors. She watched the first stars come out, thin and cold. She did not weep, and she did not eat, and she did not lie down in her gray-silk bed. She stood at the window in the dark and she thought about the man walking east with her ribbon on his wrist, and she thought about the sea, and she thought about the cottage with two rooms and a hearth and a door that stays, and she held all of it in her chest like a coal, and she let it burn.

She counted the days until midsummer. She counted the nights. And in the dark of the bedchamber, with the whole house asleep around her and the moors lying gray and empty under the stars, Lady Elara Ashworth made her vow, and she made it aloud this time, in a whisper that the walls could keep or carry as they pleased.

"I will find you," she said. "Whatever it costs. I will find you."

The wind took the words and carried them out across the moors, east, toward the sea, and the house slept on in its new silence, and on the moors a wounded man walked barefoot through the heather with a dark green ribbon tied to his wrist, and the night closed over them both, and the world turned, and nothing was the same again.

set.name: Elara Ashworth
set.description: Lady Elara Ashworth, now 20, dark-haired, sharp-eyed. She watched from her locked bedchamber window all day as Kael was flogged (fifteen strokes) and cast out barefoot through the east gate, and stood at the glass until the mist took him, then long after, until the moors were empty. She refused Margaret's tea at noon and Martha's curtains at dusk, did not eat, did not weep, did not sleep; she stood in the dark and made her vow aloud, a whisper: 'I will find you. Whatever it costs. I will find you.' She has stopped waiting for doors to open; grief has hardened into cold resolve and active war preparation, counting the days and nights to midsummer and the wedding-eve flight. Hidden flight funds intact (grandmother's pearl earrings, silver pin, coin in attic mattress seam). Her palms still carry the scored red crescents from pressing them into the stone wall. She knows her father ordered the flogging (acted on Martha's report), knows Martha's betrayal is likely, and knows the house will lie about Kael. Location: Thornwood, her gray-silk bedchamber, at the window in the dark. Goal: find Kael on the moors and flee before the midsummer wedding. Condition: transformed, resolute, prepared for war.

set.name: Lady Margaret Ashworth
set.description: Elara's mother, brittle, socially ambitious, rose-water scent. She had Elara's bedchamber door fastened at dawn, stood outside during the flogging, and retreated shaken after Elara's flat accusation ('There was no chalice... I counted every stroke'). At noon she brought tea and the seamstress's note to the locked door and got no answer; at dusk Martha found Elara standing in the dark. Margaret now knows (or strongly suspects) Elara knew the banished man and that the theft charge was false, and that her daughter has gone quiet in a way that is not grief. She will bury this knowledge and accelerate the trousseau and wedding preparations, telling herself a wedding will cure it, and will take Elara's silence for mourning over an unfortunate dalliance (chapter 19). Location: Thornwood. Goal: see her daughter married to Vexford at midsummer, keep up appearances. Condition: shaken, avoiding the truth, determined to look away.

set.name: Lord Aldous Ashworth
set.description: Elara's father, 54, tall, gaunt, gray-eyed, master of Thornwood. At dawn he publicly announced the false theft charge, ordered the fifteen-stroke flogging and banishment through the east gate with the warning that Kael will be shot if ever seen on the land or near any member of the household again. He watched Kael walk out barefoot and considers the rot cut out cleanly and the Vexford settlement salvaged. He does not know Elara watched the flogging, that her resolve has hardened into active flight planning, or that she has vowed aloud to find Kael. The household has washed the yard; the post stands empty; the name of the stable hand is not spoken. Location: Thornwood. Goal: keep the settlement intact, the house unashamed, and his daughter married at midsummer. Condition: satisfied the matter is closed; unaware of the fury and vow he has seeded in his daughter.

set.name: Martha
set.description: Sour-faced, efficient lady's maid, about thirty, deft impersonal hands, served Elara fifteen years. She arranged the betrayal (reported the affair to Ashworth, who had Kael seized and flogged) and at dawn watched Kael's punishment and casting-out. She saw Elara at the window and how the lady watched and went quiet; at dusk she came to draw the curtains and found Elara standing in the dark at the window and chose not to speak. A thread of unease runs under her satisfaction because a quiet lady is a lady she cannot read. She knows the full truth (the affair, her report, the false charge) and has told no one else. She will watch Elara's 'recovery' with cold vigilance, telling herself the danger is over. Location: Thornwood. Goal: see the household return to order; keep her place and her secret. Condition: satisfied, watchful, faintly uneasy.

set.name: Lord Vexford
set.description: Titled nobleman, 48, widower, master of Blackmoor Hall, courteous, cold, pale colorless eyes. Formally betrothed to Elara; midsummer wedding set at Blackmoor Hall. He was not present in the yard at dawn and remains unaware of Kael, the affair, the false theft charge, or the punishment. He is preparing to leave south to ready Blackmoor Hall for the wedding. Location: Thornwood (departure for Blackmoor Hall imminent). Goal: the marriage and the settlement, undisturbed.

set.name: Kael
set.description: Stable hand and groundsman at Thornwood, mid-twenties drifter, rough low voice, level gray eyes, scarred hands. At dawn he was flogged fifteen strokes at the post, cut down, given a shirt (which he dragged over his ruined back, setting the collar straight with deliberate calm) and boots he left in the mud, and a crust of bread he refused. He walked barefoot through the parted household and out the east gate onto the moors. On the moors his knees gave out and he lay on hands and knees in the mist; he got up and walked on. He stopped on a shoulder of granite and held the dark green ribbon on his wrist (stained with his blood) and let the grief crack through for a moment, then walked on, still not saying her name. In the afternoon, from a rise, he looked back once and saw Thornwood's smoke far off, stood watching until his legs shook, then turned east and did not look back again. His back is a ruin of split skin and red lattice lines, bleeding through the shirt, feet cut and bleeding; no coat, no food, no horse, no money (his hidden savings remain under the loft floor at Thornwood, unrecovered). He knows Martha betrayed them, knows the lie was for the world, knows he must never return or be killed on sight, and believes the only gift he can give Elara is his absence. Location: the open moors east of Thornwood, walking barefoot east toward the sea he has never seen. Goal: survive the moors, reach the coast, never speak her name; keep her safe by staying gone. Condition: badly flogged, bleeding, in shock, alone, walking east as the night closes in.

set.name: Steward Hale
set.description: Lord Ashworth's steward of twenty years, gray-faced, folded hands. At dawn he held Kael up when his knees buckled after the fifteenth stroke, oversaw the cutting down and the casting out, and at the gate said only 'The east gate' when Kael stopped — almost speaking something else, then closing his mouth. He watched the lady's window once and has decided to forget he saw it. Location: Thornwood. Goal: serve Lord Ashworth; maintain order. Condition: a tool who has chosen to remain a tool.

set.name: Pip
set.description: Young stable boy who sleeps in the stable loft, roughly a child in years; adores Kael. He was silenced the night before with the threat that he could hang beside Kael, and at dawn he stood at the back of the gathered servants and watched his only friend flogged and cast out barefoot. He now knows the accusation was false, is grieving and terrified, and knows no one will let him speak. Location: Thornwood stables. Goal: survive; quietly mourn. Condition: broken-hearted, silenced, powerless.

On the afternoon of his casting-out, from a rise on the eastern moors, Kael stopped and looked back once and saw Thornwood's smoke far off on the horizon; he stood watching until his legs shook, touched the ribbon on his wrist, then turned east and never looked back again.

In the dark of her locked bedchamber the night of the casting-out, Elara made her vow aloud in a whisper: 'I will find you. Whatever it costs. I will find you.' She will act on this through chapters 19-23, ending with her flight.

Kael, flogged, barefoot, coatless, and without food or money, must survive the crossing of the moors and reach the eastern coast, where he will live rough in a fishing village (chapters 24-25), so that Elara can find him there after her flight.

chapters.name: The Hollow Days
chapters.content:
The days that followed the casting-out had no names.

Elara knew this because she lay awake through so many of them that the calendar lost its meaning. She had stopped counting the days to midsummer on the night of the vow, and now the days themselves had stopped cooperating, running together like rain down a pane, gray into gray, until she could not have said whether a week had passed or a month. The only fixed things in the world were the window and the moors and the absence that stretched between them.

She refused to eat.

It was not a decision. That was the strange part, the part Martha would turn over in her mind in the weeks to come: the lady had not chosen this hunger. The food simply arrived — trays of it, under silver covers, with Margaret's own hand on the handle — and Elara looked at it, and her body declined it, the way a body declines a thing it has no use for. The first trays went back untouched. On the third day Margaret sent the white soup she had loved as a child, and then, in desperation, the honeyed apples the cook made only at Christmas, and all of it came back cold and whole, and Margaret stood in the corridor looking at the returned tray as if it had bitten her.

"She is punishing me," Margaret said to Martha in a low voice outside the door, and Martha, who had seen the lady standing in the dark with her palms scored and her eyes like open doors, said nothing at all.

Elara refused to speak.

She had spoken once, on the night of the casting-out, when she made her vow aloud in the dark — but that word was for the walls and the wind, owed to no one. To the living she gave nothing. Margaret came to the door each morning and evening, her voice bright and fraying by turns, full of seamstresses and trousseau lists and the news that Lord Vexford's steward had written again, and Elara listened to it the way she listened to the wind in the chimney. Martha came and went with curtains and jugs and clean water, and Elara did not acknowledge her. She stood at the window and looked out at the moors, and the moors looked back at her, gray and empty and indifferent.

She was searching for a shadow of a man that never appeared.

That was the whole of her occupation. From first light to last she stood at the glass and searched the eastern moors the way a sentinel searches a horizon, looking for a figure that was not there and would not be there, because she knew — with the terrible clarity of the one fact she could not argue with — that he would never come back. He had been warned that to set foot on this land again was to be shot. He was walking east toward the sea, with her ribbon on his wrist and his back in ribbons, and if he had any sense — and he had all the sense — he would keep walking and never turn around. She knew this. She had known it in the moment he walked through the east gate. And still she stood at the window every morning when the mist was thickest, when heather and fog made the whole world the color of milk, and she watched the place where the gate had been, and she waited for a shadow that never came.

She truly frightened Margaret on the fifth day.

Margaret came to the door with the seamstress's sketch, a watercolor of the wedding gown — white silk, seed pearls at the bodice, a train like a spill of cream — and talked through the panel about the alterations, and Elara did not answer, and Margaret's voice went up a note, and then another, until she said, with the particular brittleness of a woman who has run out of bright things: "Elara. You will speak to me. You will open this door and speak to me, or I shall have it broken down."

And Elara, standing at the window with her back to the door, said in a voice so flat it was almost not a voice at all: "I have nothing to say to the woman who locked me in to watch them whip him."

The silence on the other side of the door went on a very long time. Then Margaret said, in a much smaller voice: "I did not know. I swear to you, I did not know what he meant to do until the morning."

Elara did not turn around. "You knew there was no chalice. You heard me tell you there was no chalice. And you still brought me tea."

"There was no —" Margaret's voice cracked. "There was no chalice? What are you talking about? Your father said he stole it."

"My father lied. He lied to you and to the yard and to the whole county, and you let him, because it was easier than looking." Elara said it without heat, the way her father said things, and she heard Margaret's breath catch through the panel. "Go and fit the gown without me, Mama. There will be a bride in it either way. That is all this house has ever wanted from me."

Margaret did not break the door down. She went away, and the seamstress went away, and the sketch was left on the tray in the corridor until Martha picked it up and put it on the table by the door like a thing found in the road.

After that, Margaret began to tell herself the story that would carry her through the weeks. Her daughter had formed an unfortunate attachment to a servant; the servant had been caught in a theft and rightly punished; her daughter, being a young lady of feeling, was grieving the way young ladies grieved; and the wedding would cure it. Weddings cured everything. A bride had only to be put into white silk and walked down an aisle, and the past would fall away from her like a shawl, and she would become a countess and forget the stable hand as completely as if he had never existed.

"Grief over a dalliance," Margaret said to the housekeeper in the stillroom, in a voice pitched for the walls to hear. "That is all it is. A silly, girlish grief. It will pass when she is married. They always pass."

The housekeeper, who had stood in the yard at dawn and watched a man's back opened to the bone and heard the lady counting the strokes from behind a pane of glass, said, "Yes, my lady," and went back to her accounts.

And Margaret accelerated the wedding preparations.

It was the only thing she knew how to do. If the house was a wound, she would cover it with linen; if the wound was her daughter, she would cover her with silk. The preparations, which had moved at the stately pace of a great house at leisure, now acquired the desperate momentum of a ship making for harbor ahead of a storm. The seamstress was summoned for daily fittings, and when Elara would not come down, Margaret ordered the sewing moved to the corridor outside the bedchamber, so the seamstress and her girls could pin and tack within earshot of the locked door while the bride sat on the other side of the panel and watched the moors. The trousseau lists multiplied. Margaret wrote to the mercer in Merrow and the linen-draper in the county town; she ordered bolts of lawn and cambric and a dozen new nightgowns; she planned the wedding breakfast in such detail that Cook took to her bed for a day. Every letter she sealed and sent was another nail in a coffin no one would admit was being built.

Lord Ashworth ignored his daughter entirely.

That was the shape of his response, and it was as deliberate as everything he did. He did not come to the locked door. He did not ask after her. At supper he sat alone at the head of the long table with Margaret across from him, too far away for conversation, the two of them eating in the enormous silence of the great hall. When the housekeeper reported, in her careful way, that the lady had not eaten in days and would not speak, Ashworth looked at her with his flat gray eyes and said, "She will eat when she is hungry. She will speak when she has something to say. See that the wedding proceeds."

That was all. The matter of the stable hand was closed. The rot had been cut out, the yard washed, the name erased from the household's speech until the very absence of it became a kind of monument. He did not know she had watched the flogging. That was the irony that would have amused him if he had ever learned it: he had locked her in to protect her from a sight he thought too brutal for a lady, and she had watched every stroke, and the watching had unmade and remade her in the space of a gray morning, and now the woman who stood at the window was not the daughter he had raised but something harder, something with his own flat gaze and his own patience and his own absolute certainty of purpose. He would have recognized it, if he had looked. He did not look. He had cut the rot out, and he did not look back at the wound.

The servants whispered.

They whispered in the kitchen and the stillroom and on the back stair, a low constant murmur under the surface of the house, like water moving under ice. They whispered that the lady had not eaten since the morning of the flogging, that she stood at her window all day and all night, that she had gone silent in a way that was not grief. They whispered that she was cursed.

It began with the laundry maid, who had seen Elara's face at the window in the gray dawn, white as the moon, and crossed herself. Then the stories grew, fed by the cold that had settled over the house like a second season. The fires burned as they always burned, the lamps were lit as they were always lit, and yet the house was colder than it had been all winter — a cold that came from the locked room at the top of the house and seeped down the stairs like water through a ceiling. The servants drew their shawls tighter and glanced up at the second-floor window when they crossed the yard, and they whispered that the lady of the house was cursed, that she had given herself to the moors, that she would bring ruin down on them all.

Pip heard the whispers. Pip, who slept in the loft above the tack room where the other man had slept, who lay awake on straw that still smelled faintly of him, who had not spoken about anything since the morning of the flogging — Pip heard them say the lady was cursed, and he said nothing, because he knew better than anyone in the house what the curse really was. He knew there had been no chalice. He had seen Kael's face change when her shadow crossed the stable yard, seen the lady slip through the dark toward the east pasture on nights when the moon was down. He carried the truth the way he carried everything now: pressed against his ribs, silent, heavy, his mouth sealed by the threat that he could hang beside his friend.

He had taken to sleeping with the knotted cloth. It was Kael's savings, the coin hidden under the loft floor, the little hoard that was supposed to buy the cart and the mule. Pip had found it on the morning after the casting-out, when he had crawled into the empty loft to breathe the last of the smell of the only man who had ever been kind to him, and his hand had found the loose floorboard, and he had understood in a rush of terrible clarity that Kael had meant to leave, that he and the lady had meant to leave together, that this money was the door that had been slammed shut. He had tucked the cloth into his shirt and told no one. He did not know what he meant to do with it. He only knew he could not leave it for the men who had beaten his friend, and he slept with it warm against his chest, a weight like a promise he did not yet know how to keep.

Martha watched.

Martha watched the lady the way she watched everything, with cold efficient eyes and deft impersonal hands, and she told herself the danger was over. The man was gone. The secret had been delivered, the rot cut out, the household returning to order; the lady's fasting was grief, and grief passed, and the wedding would come, and Martha would keep her place, which was the only thing she had ever wanted. She told herself this every morning when she set the water jug by the lady's door, and every evening when she came to draw the curtains and found the lady standing in the dark at the window.

But the thread of unease was still there, running under her satisfaction like a splinter under a fingernail. A quiet lady was a lady she could not read. The lady did not weep — that was the thing. Martha had expected weeping, had prepared for it, knew how to hold the basin and murmur the soothing nothings and wait for the storm to pass. But the lady did not weep. She stood at the window with her scored palms and her open eyes, as still as the house was cold, and Martha could not find the seam in her, could not find the place where the grief lived and would someday break, and that frightened her more than tears would have.

"Cursed," the servants whispered, and Martha, who did not believe in curses, believed instead in what she could see: a young woman who had watched the man she loved whipped bloody and walked barefoot into the mist, who had not wept and had not eaten, who stood at the window looking east with the patience of a thing that was waiting.

Martha did not know what the lady was waiting for. She told herself it was nothing. She told herself the danger was over. And every night, before she slept, she went to the lady's door and listened, and heard nothing at all, and went away again with the splinter working a little deeper.

And Elara stood at the window.

She stood at the window through the days, and the days ran together into a single gray day with no beginning and no end. She watched the moors empty themselves of him over and over — the morning mist, the noon light, the evening gray, the dark — and she searched for a shadow that never came, and she did not eat, and she did not speak, and the coal in her chest burned steady and low, and she let it.

Because the hunger was not really hunger, and the silence was not really silence, and the hollow days were not really hollow. Something was growing in the hollow. She could feel it the way a woman feels a child quickening — a small, stubborn insistence at her center, a thing that had begun in the moment she watched the post stand empty in the courtyard and had been fed, day by day, by every returned tray and every bright voice through the panel and every whisper she could feel moving through the house beneath her like water. The house wanted her hollow. The house wanted her empty, a white silk vessel to be filled with a title and carried away. And she stood at the window and let the house think she was emptying, and all the while the thing inside her was not emptying at all — it was setting, the way a thing left out overnight sets in the frost, hardening from grief into certainty, from a vow into a plan, from a plan into a weapon.

She watched the moors, and she thought about the man walking east, and the sea he had never seen, and the cottage with two rooms and a hearth and a door that stays, and she held the coal in her chest and let it burn, and she waited.

She counted the days to midsummer. She counted the nights. And in the dark of the bedchamber, with the house asleep and the moors lying gray under the stars, she touched the scored crescents in her palms with her fingertips, and she did not say his name, because his name was a thing the house had forbidden, and she had learned long ago to keep the most important things she owned hidden in the dark where no one could take them.

She kept him there. She kept the ribbon and the sea and the door that stays, and she stood at the window in the hollow days, and she let the house believe she was breaking.

She was not breaking. She was waiting.

And the days went by, and the moors stayed empty, and Thornwood grew colder still.

set.name: Elara Ashworth
set.description: Lady Elara Ashworth, 20, dark-haired, sharp-eyed. In the hollow days following Kael's flogging and casting-out she refuses to eat (trays returned untouched; even childhood favorites sent back cold) and refuses to speak to the living (only her vow to the walls at night). She stands at her bedchamber window from first light to last, searching the eastern moors for a shadow that never appears, knowing he will never return. On day five she told Margaret through the locked door, flatly, that Margaret knew there was no chalice and let the lie stand, and that there will be a bride in the gown either way. She has not wept; grief has set inside her like frost into certainty and active war-preparation. She counts the days and nights to midsummer, holds the coal of the vow in her chest, and lets the house believe she is breaking while she is in fact waiting and hardening. Hidden flight funds intact (grandmother's pearl earrings, silver pin, coin in attic mattress seam). Palms still scored with red crescents. She knows the house will lie about Kael and does not speak his name to anyone. Location: Thornwood, gray-silk bedchamber, at the window. Goal: endure the hollow days, appear broken, then move about the house and prepare to flee on the night before the midsummer wedding. Condition: emaciated, sleepless, resolute, waiting.

set.name: Lady Margaret Ashworth
set.description: Elara's mother, brittle, socially ambitious, rose-water scent. During the hollow days she brought daily trays (including white soup and honeyed apples), talked wedding details through the locked door, and on day five heard Elara's flat accusation that there was no chalice and that Margaret had let the lie stand; Margaret protested she had not known until the morning. She did not break the door down. She now tells herself the story that Elara grieves an unfortunate dalliance with a servant and that the wedding will cure it, and she accelerates the trousseau and wedding preparations feverishly (daily fittings moved to the corridor outside the locked door, letters to the mercer and linen-draper, planning the wedding breakfast) to cover scandal. Location: Thornwood. Goal: see her daughter married to Vexford at midsummer, keep up appearances, outrun scandal. Condition: shaken, avoiding the truth, clinging to the wedding as cure.

set.name: Lord Aldous Ashworth
set.description: Elara's father, 54, tall, gaunt, gray-eyed, master of Thornwood. During the hollow days he entirely ignores his daughter: he does not come to the locked door, does not ask after her, and told the housekeeper flatly that she will eat when hungry, speak when she has something to say, and that the wedding proceeds. He believes the rot is cut out and the matter closed. He does not know Elara watched the flogging and is hardening into a weapon; the irony is that the daughter standing at the window now has his own flat gaze, patience, and certainty of purpose, which he would recognize only if he looked. Location: Thornwood, dining alone at the head of the long table. Goal: keep the settlement intact and the wedding on schedule. Condition: satisfied the matter is closed; blind to the resolve he seeded.

set.name: Martha
set.description: Sour-faced, efficient lady's maid, about thirty, deft impersonal hands. During the hollow days she brings water and draws curtains, watching Elara's fasting and silence with cold vigilance. She tells herself the danger is over and the household is returning to order, but a thread of unease runs under her satisfaction: the lady does not weep, and a quiet lady is one Martha cannot read or find the seam of; she listens at the door at night and hears nothing. She knows the full truth (the affair, her report, the false charge) and has told no one else. Location: Thornwood. Goal: see the household return to order and keep her place and secret. Condition: satisfied, watchful, faintly uneasy.

set.name: Lord Vexford
set.description: Titled nobleman, 48, widower, master of Blackmoor Hall, courteous, cold, pale colorless eyes. Formally betrothed to Elara; midsummer wedding set at Blackmoor Hall. Absent from Thornwood and unaware of Kael, the affair, the false charge, or the punishment; his steward has written again about the wedding arrangements. Location: preparing to leave south to ready Blackmoor Hall for the wedding. Goal: the marriage and settlement, undisturbed.

set.name: Kael
set.description: Stable hand and groundsman, mid-twenties drifter, rough low voice, level gray eyes, scarred hands, dark green ribbon on his wrist. Cast out barefoot through the east gate after fifteen lashes; walking east across the moors toward the sea, surviving on streams and whatever the land offers, back a lattice of healing wounds, feet cut. No coat, no food, no money (savings still hidden under the loft floor at Thornwood, now in Pip's keeping). He believes the only gift he can give Elara is his absence and will never return or be killed on sight. Location: the open moors east of Thornwood, moving east. Goal: survive, reach the eastern coast, never speak her name. Condition: wounded, healing, alone, walking.

set.name: Steward Hale
set.description: Lord Ashworth's steward of twenty years, gray-faced, folded hands. In the hollow days he goes about his duties maintaining order; he saw the lady's window once and has decided to forget he saw it, and he does not speak the banished man's name. Location: Thornwood. Goal: serve Lord Ashworth; keep the household running toward the wedding. Condition: a tool who has chosen to remain a tool.

set.name: Pip
set.description: Young stable boy who sleeps in the stable loft, roughly a child in years; adores Kael. In the hollow days he hears the servants whisper that the lady is cursed and says nothing, carrying the truth (no chalice, the lovers' nightly meetings) pressed against his ribs, mouth sealed by the threat of hanging. On the morning after the casting-out he found Kael's hidden savings (the knotted cloth of coin under the loft floor) and took it, keeping it warm against his chest; he does not know what he will do with it, only that he will not leave it for the men who beat his friend. Location: Thornwood stables. Goal: survive; keep the cloth safe. Condition: broken-hearted, grieving, silent, holding Kael's savings.

In the days after the casting-out, Elara refused to eat (all trays returned untouched, including childhood favorites sent by Margaret) and refused to speak to anyone; she stood at her bedchamber window from first light to last searching the eastern moors for a shadow of Kael that never appeared. On day five she told Margaret through the locked door, flatly, that Margaret had known there was no chalice and let the lie stand, and that there would be a bride in the gown either way; Margaret retreated shaken and thereafter told herself the story that Elara grieved an unfortunate dalliance and that the wedding would cure it.

Lady Margaret, fearing scandal and taking Elara's silence for grief over a dalliance, accelerated the wedding preparations with desperate momentum: daily gown fittings moved to the corridor outside the locked bedchamber, letters to the mercer in Merrow and the linen-draper, a multiplied trousseau, and detailed wedding-breakfast planning that sent Cook to her bed for a day.

Lord Ashworth ignored his daughter entirely during the hollow days: he did not visit the locked door or ask after her, ate alone at the head of the long table, and told the housekeeper flatly that she will eat when hungry and speak when she has something to say, and that the wedding proceeds. He remains unaware that she watched the flogging and is hardening into a weapon.

The servants began to whisper that the lady of the house is cursed: that she has not eaten since the morning of the flogging, stands at her window all day and night, and has gone silent in a way that is not grief; a coldness has settled over Thornwood like a second season, seeping down from the locked room.
