During the hard winter, with the house heavy with his presence and his wife a ghost, Vexford began to look at the maids and has set his eye on the new red-haired kitchen maid, who looks back bold as brass; the cook reported it to Mrs. Carrick in the larder and the whisper spread through the house, everyone waiting for the lady to storm — and no storm comes, because Elara heard it and felt nothing at all.

In the deep of the night, when her husband is away and the house sleeps, Elara sometimes takes the satchel from the bottom of her trunk — rope, tinderbox, brandy, grandmother's pearl earrings, silver pin, saved coin, the stolen Thornwood rear-door key — and holds it without opening it, the archaeology of the life that ended on a cliff by the sea, then puts it back and watches the moors until dawn.

By the end of the first year Lord Vexford will have taken the red-haired kitchen maid as his mistress, as he did with his first wife; the servants wait to see the lady's reaction, and Elara will feel neither jealousy nor anger nor relief — only a quiet numbness (chapter 35).

The red-haired kitchen maid, once she becomes Vexford's mistress, remains in the household and becomes part of the year's whisper; her fate and Elara's indifference toward her echo the pattern of the first wife and feed the house's talk that the lady is cursed (chapters 35-36).

chapters.name: The Walking Ghost
chapters.content:
By the end of the first year, the household of Blackmoor Hall no longer waited for the lady to storm. The waiting had worn itself out, month after month, the way the moors wore down every storm that crossed them, until the servants simply accepted the new shape of the house as they had accepted the new shape of its mistress: without comment, with only the resigned patience of people who have learned that a great house goes on regardless.

The shape of the house was this: the lord kept a mistress.

It had begun, as such things begin, without announcement. The red-haired kitchen maid — her name was Molly, come up from the village at Michaelmas with a face like a milkmaid in a song and eyes that wanted things — ceased, at some point in the late autumn, to be a kitchen maid. The change was not spoken of. There was no scene, no dismissal, no public declaration. The girl was simply seen, more and more, in the parts of the house where the lord was, and then — the whisper moved through the house like a draft — in the lord's own rooms of an evening, when the rest of the household was below.

Mrs. Carrick handled it as she handled everything: without acknowledgment. She had managed Blackmoor Hall for twenty years and three mistresses, and she had seen the first wife die of a broken thing no physician could name, and she had watched the new lady run the house like a clock. She did not speak of the red-haired girl. She did not need to. The house spoke of her, in the kitchen and the larder, in the low voices of servants who have learned to say everything while saying nothing.

"Her own lady," the cook said to Mrs. Carrick one evening in the pantry, low and bitter, "up in the east tower at her window, and that girl—" She could not finish.

"The mistress and the girl," Mrs. Carrick said. "Near enough the same age."

"Age has nothing to do with it. The one's got nothing and wants everything. The other's got everything and wants nothing. It's a bad trade for the house." The cook crossed herself, a habit worn smooth as a stone. "He broke the first one. He'll break this one too."

Mrs. Carrick said nothing. She remembered the first wife — a pretty, frightened girl who had cried through her first winter — and the six years of the sealed room, and the second wife arriving with nothing, running everything, wanting nothing. She thought of the lady at the east-tower window at dusk, hands folded, face empty, watching the moors like someone waiting for a boat that isn't coming.

"He won't break this one," she said at last, and could not say why she was certain, only that she was. "This one's already gone. He can't break what isn't there."

The whisper, as whispers do, reached Elara.

She heard it the way she heard everything now — mechanically, without interest, the way a clock hears the striking of other clocks. She heard that her husband had taken the red-haired kitchen maid into his rooms, that the girl had been given a silk wrapper and a room near the lord's chambers, that the servants waited to see what the lady would do. She heard it all, in the stillroom and the corridor, in the hush that fell when she passed, and she felt nothing at all.

She had known it would happen. She had known it the way she knew the shape of a ledger. He was a man who liked warmth, and she was a cold room, and the arithmetic was as simple as any sum in the books she balanced every evening at seven. She had expected to feel something when it came — jealousy, perhaps, or anger, or at least the small sour satisfaction of being right. But when it came, there was nothing. The event arrived and passed through her like weather through an empty house, leaving no mark on the walls.

She did not hate the girl. Hatred would have required her to care that the girl existed. She looked at Molly once, across the kitchen yard on a gray afternoon — a pretty girl with red hair and a frightened, defiant mouth, alive in a way that Elara had once been alive, wanting things in a way that Elara had once wanted things — and she felt nothing at all.

She wished the girl well, in the same flat way she wished her husband well when he rode out. She hoped the girl would give him whatever he needed that she could not, would not be broken the way the one before her had been broken, the one whose room she slept in. She hoped it the way one hopes for fair weather, without stake in the outcome.

When Mrs. Carrick, delicately, in the stillroom, in the careful way of housekeepers who must know where the storm is, said, "My lady, there is talk in the house — about the lord and the girl—" Elara looked up from the larder list in her hand and said, "Yes," and went on looking at the list.

Mrs. Carrick waited. Nothing came.

"Will you—" Mrs. Carrick began, and stopped. She did not know what she had meant to ask. Will you dismiss her? Will you weep? Will you do anything at all?

"No," Elara said, to the question she had not finished asking. "I won't. She does no harm. I hope he is kind to her."

Mrs. Carrick stood very still. In twenty years and three mistresses she had heard a wife learn of a mistress and weep, rage, faint, take to her bed, or dismiss the girl. She had never heard one say, in a soft even voice, without a flicker of anything, I hope he is kind to her.

"My lady," she said, and her voice came out rougher than she meant. "You are the mistress of this house."

"Yes," Elara said. "I am. The accounts are balanced, the larder is mended, the arrears are closed. That is what a mistress is for." She set the list down and looked at Mrs. Carrick with her flat gray eyes. "The rest of it — that was never mine. It was never mine to keep."

Mrs. Carrick did not understand, and understood that she was not meant to, and went back to her work, and the whisper settled a little, and the house went on.

Lord Vexford, for his part, was almost content.

He had his mistress, warm and willing and young, and she looked at him with eyes that wanted things — his attention, his favor, his rooms, his name, in time, perhaps. He gave her the silk wrapper and the room and the glances, and took his warmth from her, and it was good, in the way warmth is good to a man who has been sitting in a cold room for a year. He was not a cruel man, or not deliberately; he had broken his first wife the way a man breaks a horse by riding it too hard, without ever noticing the breaking. He did not intend to break Molly. He intended, vaguely, to enjoy her, and to be kind, in his way, which was the way of a man who is kind to things he owns.

And yet. He could not quite stop watching his wife.

He had told himself, through the winter, that the puzzle of her would resolve itself — that she would crack, or soften, or at least do something. A year had passed, and she had done none of it. She was flawless and she was absent, and now she knew about Molly — everyone knew about Molly; the house had hummed with it for weeks, waiting for the storm — and she had done nothing. She had not dismissed the girl. She had not wept. She had not even looked at him differently. She had wished him well when he left for his evenings, and she had meant it.

The splinter in his mind settled into a fixed and baffling certainty: his wife did not care. Not that he had taken a mistress — that he could have understood, could have managed, could have endured her rage or her tears with the satisfaction of a man who has won a point. She did not care about anything. He could have burned the house down around her and she would have balanced the ashes in her ledger and thanked him for the warmth.

He sat in his study one evening, Molly dismissed to her rooms, and turned the thought over, and could not make it fit. He was a man who had always assumed that everyone wanted what he wanted — warmth, comfort, position, the small satisfactions of being obeyed and envied. He could not imagine a person who wanted nothing, for whom the world had become a gray glass through which she watched, unmoved, the whole of her life happening to someone else.

It's as if she's already dead, he thought, and did not say it aloud. It's as if I married a walking ghost.

And so the house settled into its new shape: the lord with his mistress, the lady at her window, the servants moving between them like water between two stones, careful, silent, expecting nothing. The dinner table had an empty place that was not empty. The lady smiled her cued bell-sound when the conversation required it, and the house ran like a clock, and the clock did not strike.

Elara spent her days at the east-tower window.

It was not a choice. It was not even a habit. It was simply where she was, the way a stone is where it lies. The window faced the moors — gray, endless, empty, the same moors she had watched from a cold window at Thornwood as a girl, the same moors she had crossed on a gray horse with a wanted man for six days of flight, the same moors that had funneled her, at the last, to a cliff's edge and a black sea. She had thought, once, that the moors were a cage. She understood now that they were not a cage. They were the only thing that had never lied to her.

The landscape had become her only company.

She watched it the way other women watched their children, or their gardens, or the faces of their husbands — with attention, with patience, with the particular devotion of a person who has nothing else. She watched the light change over the heather from gray to silver to gray. She watched the weather come in from the sea, long veils of rain moving across the distances. She watched the wind lay the grass down and let it up again, in a rhythm as patient as breath. She watched the seasons turn — the heather bloom and fade, the snow lock the land, the thaw run silver in the ditches, the heather bloom again — and she felt, in the presence of the moors, the only thing she had left that was not numbness.

It was not peace. It was not hope. It was something quieter, something that asked nothing of her: the sense that the moors understood her, because they too were a gray emptiness that went on and on and did not care. She was the moors' mirror, and they were hers, and it was the only company she could bear.

She did not think of the cottage. She had learned, through the year, the exact geography of the place in her mind that she must not approach — the door that stays, the hearth, the fire lit at dusk, the heather garden, the children with his steady hands and her sharp eyes, the daughter named Anna. She knew where it was, the way a woman knows where a grave is, and she walked around it the way she walked around the locked rooms of the house at night: carefully, in the dark, without looking in. If she looked in, the husk of her would crack, and what was inside would spill out and drown her, and she had promised him the fire at dusk, and a woman who has promised a dead man a fire at dusk cannot afford to drown.

So she did not think of the cottage. She thought of the moors.

Sometimes, in the deep of the night, when her husband was with his mistress and the house was asleep, she took the satchel from the bottom of her trunk — the rope, the tinderbox, the brandy, her grandmother's pearl earrings, the silver pin, the saved coin, the stolen key to a door she would never again need — and held it without opening it. The archaeology of a dead life. She had stopped asking why she kept it. It was the only evidence that the woman who had ridden east on a gray horse had ever existed, and she kept it the way she kept the green ribbon at her wrist, because there was no one else to keep either of them.

She tied the ribbon each morning, before anything else, under her sleeve. It had faded from green to a gray-green the color of the moors, worn thin as a whisper by a year of her wrist, and she had thought, once, that she should put it away before it wore through and was lost, and she had not. She wanted it to wear through. She wanted it to become nothing, gradually, the way everything became nothing, so that when it was finally gone she would not have to notice it going.

It had not gone. It held. She held it. The fire at dusk, she thought. The fire at dusk.

It was winter again when the household noticed, in the way households notice everything, that the lady had grown thinner.

It was not dramatic. There was no collapse, no locked door. She simply ate less — a few spoonfuls of soup, a corner of bread — and slept less, though no one could have said how they knew, since she rose before the light regardless and went to bed at the same hour, in the dead woman's room, alone now, most nights, her husband having taken to his mistress's rooms with a regularity that had become, in its way, a kind of order. She walked the cold halls at night, barefoot, and the servants who saw her — and they saw her, though she thought herself unseen — crossed themselves and said nothing.

"She's at her window," Mrs. Carrick said to the cook, in the larder, in the particular hush of the deep winter. "Morning to night, near enough. She doesn't ring for anything. She doesn't eat. She doesn't—" She stopped.

"Doesn't what?"

"Doesn't anything," Mrs. Carrick said. "She's not waiting anymore. She was waiting before. You could see it in her, like a held breath. Now the breath's let go."

The cook crossed herself. "For what, then?"

"Nothing," Mrs. Carrick said. "I think she's stopped waiting for anything at all. I think she's just—" She searched for the word and did not find it. "Watching."

"She's a ghost," the cook said. "A walking ghost. We've all said it. The lord with his girl, and the lady a ghost at her window, and the house colder for it. Something was taken out of that one and nothing put back. Nothing ever will be put back."

Mrs. Carrick was silent. She had managed the house for twenty years and three mistresses, and she had seen the first wife die, and she had thought she understood the house and its lord. She had been wrong. She understood only that the lady was at the east-tower window, watching the moors, and that the moors were gray and endless and empty, and that the lady was becoming, slowly, as gray and endless and empty as they were.

"She wears something," Mrs. Carrick said at last, slowly, as if remembering. "On her wrist. Under her sleeve. I saw it once, when she reached for a book and the sleeve rode up. A ribbon. Green, or it was green once. Faded now, gray-green, like the moors."

"Whose?" the cook asked.

Mrs. Carrick did not answer. She thought of the lady who had arrived with nothing — no trunks, no servants, no anything — and of the ribbon she wore under her sleeve like a wound, and of the window where she sat, and of the sea beyond the moors, and she understood, without being able to say it, that the lady was keeping something alive that everyone else in the world had agreed to let die.

"She's keeping it," Mrs. Carrick said. "Whatever it is. She's keeping it, and it's the only thing she's keeping, and when it's gone—" She stopped.

The cook waited.

"When it's gone," Mrs. Carrick said, "I think she'll go too."

The winter passed, and the moors held the snow, and the house ran like a clock that had forgotten how to strike, and the lord kept his mistress and his cold courtesy and his growing, baffled certainty that he was married to a walking ghost. And Elara sat at the east-tower window and watched the light change over the endless gray, and felt nothing at all, and kept her fire lit at dusk in the only way she had left.

She was his shore. She would be, every dusk, forever.

It was the only thing left of her that was still alive.

She watches the lady at the east-tower window at dusk month after month, thinner now, eating less, 'like someone waiting for a boat that isn't coming.' Goal: serve the house and its strange mistress properly, and fearfully. Condition: obedient, uneasy, quietly awed, frightened for the lady, at Blackmoor Hall.

set.name: Molly
set.description: Molly, the red-haired kitchen maid come up from the village at Michaelmas, about Elara's age, a face like a milkmaid in a song and eyes that want things. By the end of the first year she has become Lord Vexford's mistress: a silk wrapper, a room near his chambers, a place at the edge of the household's whisper. She is frightened and defiant, bold as brass, alive in a way Elara once was, wanting things — his attention, his favor, his rooms, in time perhaps his name. Elara wishes her well flatly and hopes Vexford will not break her as he broke the first wife; the servants wait for the lady to storm and no storm comes. Goal: keep the lord's favor, rise in the house, survive. Condition: young, hopeful, frightened, alive, at Blackmoor Hall.

By the end of the first year Lord Vexford formally took the red-haired kitchen maid Molly as his mistress: a silk wrapper, a room near his chambers, no public declaration; he sleeps in her rooms most nights, is almost content, and thinks of his wife as 'a walking ghost' because she did not care.

Elara heard the whisper of the mistress and felt nothing at all — not jealousy, not anger, not even relief; she looked at Molly across the kitchen yard once and wished her well flatly, and told Mrs. Carrick 'I hope he is kind to her' and 'the rest of it was never mine to keep.'

Through the deep winter of her first year at Blackmoor Hall Elara's secret decline began: she ate less, slept less, grew thinner, and spent her days at the east-tower window watching the gray moors, which became her only company, a mirror of her emptiness; the green ribbon on her wrist faded to gray-green and she deliberately did not put it away, wanting it to wear through gradually.

Mrs. Carrick saw the faded green ribbon under Elara's sleeve and understood the lady is keeping something alive that everyone else has agreed to let die; she told the cook the lady is not waiting anymore but just watching, and that when the ribbon is gone she thinks Elara will go too.

Through the winter into the spring of her second year at Blackmoor Hall, Elara's secret decline continues — she eats less, sleeps less, her dresses hang loose on her frame, and she replays every moment with Kael from their first meeting to his silent fall — and she begins to think of Raven's Point not as a place of horror but as a place where she might feel near him again (chapter 36).

chapters.name: The East Tower Window
chapters.content:
The decline began in secret, the way all true declines begin: with small surrenders that looked, to anyone watching, like nothing at all.

Elara did not announce it. She did not take to her bed, did not lock her door, did not refuse the tray the way she had refused the trays at Thornwood, when refusal had been a weapon she could still hold. That had been an act of war. This was not war. This was the slow, quiet business of a thing that had decided, at last, to stop holding on, and it moved through her the way the thaw moved through the moors in spring — not by violence, but by a patient loosening, a giving way that the eye could not catch in any single hour but that the weeks made unmistakable.

She ate less.

It was not a choice, or if it was, it was a choice so small and so repeated that it had stopped feeling like one. A few spoonfuls of soup. A corner of bread. The small even spoonfuls that had once been the discipline of endurance became, gradually, a discipline of something else. She sat at the head of his table and moved the food around her plate with the mechanical exactness she brought to everything now, and the servants cleared her plate and noted, in the way servants note everything, that it came back more full each week than the week before. The cook began to send up her own soft things — custards, jellies, little cakes that a wasting appetite might take — and they came back barely touched, and Mrs. Carrick said nothing, and the house went on.

She slept less.

She had never slept much, not since the cliff. But now even the shallow sleep of the dead woman's room began to desert her. She lay in the dark and listened to the house settle and the wind cross the moors, and she watched the slow gray change of the window from black to first light, and she rose before the light and began again, as she had always risen, and the hours she spent at the east-tower window lengthened until they were nearly all of her days.

The dresses hung loose on her frame.

It was Mrs. Carrick who noticed it first, in the way she noticed everything — in the fold of a gown at the lady's waist as she passed through the stillroom, in the way the shoulder seams sat, in the small particular geometry of cloth on a body that is leaving itself. The lady had arrived thin; she had been thinner through the winter; now the gowns themselves betrayed her. The seamstress was summoned, and the lady stood patient as a tailor's dummy while the pins went in, and she said, in her soft even voice, "Take them in, then. It does not matter," and Mrs. Carrick heard in that the same sound she had heard in the stillroom the day of the mistress — the sound of a woman to whom the fit of her own clothes no longer signified anything at all.

The moors called to her.

That was how she had come to think of it, in the deep hours, though she would not have used the word called, because calling implied a voice, and the moors had no voice. They had a presence, a pull, the particular gravity of a thing that is vast and gray and patient and does not care. She had thought once, as a girl at Thornwood, that the moors were a cage, and she had learned on the flight that they were a road, and now she understood that they were something else again: they were the country where all of it had happened, the only place left in the world that still held him.

She watched them from the east-tower window and they watched her back, gray and endless, and in the spring light they were a sea.

That was the word she came to. A sea of heather and memory. The heather was not yet in bloom — it was early spring, and the hills wore the dun and gray of the year's turning — but she could feel the bloom coming, the way she could feel everything about that land now, with the particular intimacy of a woman who has crossed it on foot and on horseback and in terror and in love. She knew its fold and its hollows. She knew where the light went in and did not come out. She knew the smell of it after rain and the sound of it in the wind, and she watched it the way she had once watched a man's hands move across a page, with an attention so complete that it had become, without her noticing, the whole of her life.

And because the moors were the country where all of it had happened, they began, gently, to undo the careful keeping of her mind.

She had kept the cottage walled off all year. She had walked around it the way she walked around the locked rooms at night, in the dark, without looking in. But the moors would not let her keep it so. The moors held the road, and the road held the flight, and the flight held him, and one gray afternoon, watching the light move across the heather, she let herself remember.

It came back in order, the way such things come back when the keeping finally lets go: not as grief, but as story. She had been afraid, once, that remembering would drown her. But the water did not come. What came instead was a strange, terrible clarity, as if she had been watching her life through a fog for a year and the fog had thinned.

She remembered the first time she saw him.

It was autumn at Thornwood — a cold wind out of the moors, a yard full of men, and a black stallion that had come in from the summer fair wild and vicious, the terror of the grooms. And a drifter with no name standing in the middle of the yard, patient as the land itself, and the wild thing settling under his hands the way a storm settles, slowly, into the shape of the country it crosses. She had watched from a frost-rimed window and had felt a locked door open a crack inside her, and she had not known, then, that she was watching the man she would love for the rest of her life. She had thought she was watching a horse come to its senses.

She remembered the dying mare.

It had been a bitter winter morning, and she had slipped into the stables to escape the house and found him sitting with the old gray carriage mare that the grooms had abandoned and the steward had ordered put down. He had sat with her through the freezing night, murmuring to her with gentle hands, and the mare had died at dawn in the presence of the only person in the world who had stayed to see her go. Elara had stood in the shadow of the stall door and watched a servant keep a vigil for a horse that no one owned, and she had wept silently, for the first time in years, and she had vowed she would not live a life that died alone and unmarked. She had not known she was promising him, then, that she would not let him die alone. But she had kept that promise, in the end, in the only way left to her: she had made sure the world would remember him, even if the world never knew his name.

She remembered the library.

The cold, north-facing room, the rain-stained book, the candle stub, the laborious mouthing of words by a man who had forgotten his letters over twenty years of wandering. She remembered the way his hands had hovered over the page, the way they had nearly touched hers, the way he had said that all any man wants is to be known that he was here in the world, and the way she had answered, I know you are here. She remembered the first snow, and the touch on the doorframe that neither of them had drawn away from, and the hunting lodge in the storm, and the first kiss that was a dam breaking after months of near-touches, and the ribbon she had tied on his wrist in the dark, promising him a home in her that no world could take.

She remembered the cottage.

It came to her now in its whole shape, the way it had come to her on the fifth night of the flight in the cellar of the ruined chapel, and she did not turn away from it, and it did not drown her. Two rooms and a hearth. A door that stays. A heather garden with her own turnip rows. A fire lit at dusk, and a man at the sea's edge watching the road inland, and children with his steady hands and her sharp eyes, and a daughter named Anna after the grandmother who had given her the pearl earrings that still lay at the bottom of her trunk. It had been real. It had been more real than any of this — the east tower, the dead woman's room, the cold courtesy of a man who slept in another woman's bed. The cottage had been built between them word by word in the dark, and it existed still, somewhere, the way a thing exists that has been loved into being, and she had promised him the fire at dusk, and the fire at dusk was the only thing she had left to keep.

She remembered the sea.

She had seen it for the first time on the last day of the flight, gray and endless and alive, breaking on the rocks below a narrow cliff path, with the hidden village's smoke rising from a cut between two headlands — the dream she had carried out of a cold library, real and almost within reach, and then her father cresting the hill behind them and the crescent of riders closing like a net. She remembered Raven's Point, and the wind, and the fourteen horsemen, and her father's voice offering Kael one gift: walk to the edge and step off, and I will tell her you fell. And she remembered Kael pulling the ribbon from his wrist and throwing it to her on the rock, and stepping backward into the void in silence, and the black sea swallowing him.

She had thought, all through the year, that Raven's Point was the worst place in the world.

She had thought of it as the place where everything had ended, the place she must never approach in her mind, the place that had taken him. She had kept it walled off with the cottage and the door that stays and Anna, all of it together, all of it unbearable.

But the moors, in their patience, had other lessons.

And on an afternoon in the early spring, watching the light move across the gray, she understood something she had not understood before: that Raven's Point was not the place where she had lost him. It was the place where he had been nearest to her in all the world. It was the place where he had stood with her and held her hand and said It looks like you, and laughed his rusty chapel-cellar laugh, and chosen her — chosen her freedom, chosen her survival, chosen to be her shore by giving himself to the sea so that she could go on. It was the last place on earth where she had been loved.

She had been so afraid of the place. She had kept it at the far edge of her mind like a wound she could not touch. And now, sitting at the east-tower window with the moors gray and endless before her, she felt the fear loosen, the way everything in her had been loosening all spring, and she understood that the place was not horror. It was the only place left in the world where she could feel near him.

She began to think of it.

Not as a destination. Not yet. She did not make plans; she had made plans once, and the plans had ended on a cliff, and she had no plans left in her. It was not even a decision. It was a turning, the slow drift of a thing that has come loose from its moorings and is moving, at last, in the direction of the current. She sat at the window and watched the moors, and she thought of the walk to Raven's Point — three hours across the heather, she had worked it out without meaning to, from the gate of Blackmoor to the spur of rock where the land gives up — and she thought of standing at the edge where he had taken his final step, and of the wind, and of the sea, and of being, for one moment, in the only place that still held him.

She did not think of it as death.

That was the strange mercy of it. She had stopped thinking in those terms, or perhaps she had started thinking in other terms altogether. The moors called to her, and she understood now that what they were calling her toward was not an ending. It was a reunion. It was the place where she had been nearest to him, and she was going to stand there again, and breathe the salt air, and be, for an hour, not the mistress of Blackmoor Hall with her dead eyes and her balanced ledgers, but the woman he had loved, the woman who had promised him a fire at dusk, the woman who was his shore.

The ribbon at her wrist had faded to a gray-green the color of the moors, worn thin as a whisper by a year and more of her wrist, and she had wanted it to wear through gradually so she would not have to notice it going. It had not gone. It held. She held it. And now, watching the moors, she understood that the ribbon would not wear through in time, and that she did not want it to — that when she stood at the edge of the rock at Raven's Point, she wanted to be wearing it, the way he had worn hers on his wrist through the six days of flight, the way they had carried each other's promises across the whole of that gray country and down to the sea.

She was his shore. She would be, every dusk, forever.

And in the spring, as the heather began to stir toward bloom across the endless moors, she sat at the east-tower window and watched the light move over the gray sea of it, and she let herself remember everything, and she felt, for the first time in more than a year, something other than numbness.

It was not peace. It was not hope. It was quieter than either, and it asked nothing of her, and it had a direction.

She would go to Raven's Point.

Not today. Perhaps not soon. But the thought had taken root in her the way the heather took root in the moor, slowly, invisibly, and it was growing, and she watched the moors with new eyes — the eyes of a woman who knew, at last, where she was going, and who had stopped being afraid of the only place in the world that still held the man she loved.

Mrs. Carrick found her there at dusk, in the dark, with her hands folded and her face empty, and she did not know that anything had changed. She saw only the lady at the east-tower window, thinner than she had been at Candlemas, watching the moors the way she always watched the moors, and she went back down to the kitchen and told the cook, in a low voice, that the lady was still at her window, and that she had not rung for anything, and that the ribbon was still there, faded gray-green, holding on.

"Still holding," the cook said.

"Still holding," Mrs. Carrick agreed. But she had a strange feeling, that evening, that she could not have named: the feeling that the lady had not, after all, stopped waiting, but that she had finished waiting for the boat, and had begun, in some quiet way, to think of walking out to meet it.

The spring deepened. The heather stirred. And in the east tower of Blackmoor Hall, a woman who had promised a dead man a fire at dusk sat at her window and watched the moors, and remembered every moment of the man she had loved from the first time she saw him to the last, and let the moors carry her, at last, toward the only place where she could feel near him again.

She was his shore. She would be, every dusk, forever.

It was the only thing left of her that was still alive, and it was enough, and it was moving, slowly, across the gray sea of heather and memory, toward the place where the land gives up.

set.name: Elara Ashworth
set.description: Now Lady Elara Vexford, 21, dark-haired, at Blackmoor Hall, a walking ghost. Her secret decline has deepened through the early spring of her second year: she eats less (a few spoonfuls of soup, a corner of bread; the cook's soft foods come back barely touched), sleeps less, and her dresses hang loose on her frame — the seamstress was summoned and Elara said flatly 'Take them in, then. It does not matter.' Her days are spent almost entirely at the east-tower window of the dead first wife's room watching the gray moors, which she has come to see as a sea of heather and memory. This spring the moors undid her careful keeping: she let herself remember everything, in order, from her first sight of Kael calming the black stallion at Thornwood, through the dying mare, the library lessons, the first snow, the hunting lodge, the ribbon, the cottage dream (two rooms, a hearth, a door that stays, heather, children, Anna), the flight, the first sight of the sea, and his silent fall at Raven's Point — and it did not drown her. She has reframed Raven's Point: no longer the place of horror where she lost him, but the last place on earth where she was loved and the only place where she can feel near him again; she wants to be wearing the faded gray-green ribbon when she stands there. It is not yet a plan, but a quiet turning — she has worked out (without meaning to) that it is a three-hour walk from the gate of Blackmoor to the spur of rock where the land gives up, and she has begun to think of walking out to meet the boat rather than waiting for it. She still runs the household mechanically (accounts balanced nightly at seven, arrears closed since Candlemas), still walks the cold halls at night barefoot, still keeps the satchel at the bottom of her trunk (rope, tinderbox, brandy, grandmother's pearl earrings, silver pin, saved coin, the stolen Thornwood rear-door key) without opening it, and still keeps her promise to light the fire at dusk by staying alive as the one who knows. She felt nothing when Vexford took Molly as his mistress and still wishes the girl well flatly. Goal: keep Kael's memory alive, keep the fire at dusk forever, and reach Raven's Point to stand where he stood. Condition: broken, hollow, mechanically perfect, utterly absent, declining in secret with a new quiet direction; Mrs. Carrick senses she has stopped waiting for the boat and begun thinking of walking out to meet it.

set.name: Mrs. Carrick
set.description: Mrs. Carrick, housekeeper of Blackmoor Hall, twenty years in post and three mistresses before Elara, gray-haired, capable, wary. She noticed the lady's decline first — the fold of a gown at the waist, shoulder seams sitting wrong, the dresses hanging loose on the lady's frame — and summoned the seamstress, and heard the lady say flatly 'Take them in, then. It does not matter,' the same empty sound she heard the day of the mistress. She continues to manage a house that runs like a clock under the new lady, handling the lord's mistress Molly without acknowledgment. She still sees the faded gray-green ribbon under the lady's sleeve and still believes that when the ribbon is gone the lady will go too, but this spring she has a strange new feeling she cannot name: that the lady has not stopped waiting after all, but has finished waiting for the boat that isn't coming, and has begun, in some quiet way, to think of walking out to meet it. She watches the lady at the east-tower window at dusk, thinner than at Candlemas, and told the cook the ribbon is still holding on. Goal: serve the house and its strange mistress properly, and fearfully. Condition: obedient, uneasy, quietly awed, frightened for the lady, at Blackmoor Hall.

In the early spring of her second year at Blackmoor Hall, Elara's secret decline sharpened: she eats less (cook's custards and jellies come back barely touched), sleeps less, and her dresses hang loose on her frame; the seamstress was summoned and Elara said flatly 'Take them in, then. It does not matter.'

One gray afternoon the moors undid Elara's careful keeping and she let herself remember everything, in order, from her first sight of Kael calming the black stallion, through the dying mare, the library lessons, the first snow and the doorframe touch, the hunting lodge and first kiss, the ribbon, the cottage dream (two rooms, a hearth, a door that stays, children, Anna), the flight, the first sight of the sea, and his silent fall at Raven's Point; it did not drown her but gave her a strange, terrible clarity.

Elara came to understand that Raven's Point is not where she lost Kael but the last place on earth where she was loved and the only place where she can feel near him again; she has begun to think of it not as death but as reunion, and has worked out (without meaning to) that it is a three-hour walk from the gate of Blackmoor to the spur of rock where the land gives up, wanting to wear the faded ribbon when she stands there. It is not yet a plan, but a quiet turning toward the current.

On the anniversary of Kael's death Elara will walk alone to Raven's Point, a three-hour journey through the moors from the gate of Blackmoor Hall, stand at the cliff edge where he took his final step, breathe the salt air and find a strange peace without jumping or weeping, then return to Blackmoor and take to her bed, not to rise again (chapter 37).

Elara resolved that she wants to be wearing Kael's faded gray-green ribbon when she stands at the edge of the rock at Raven's Point, the way he wore hers through the flight; the ribbon's fate at the cliff matters for the anniversary walk (chapter 37).

chapters.name: The Anniversary
chapters.content:
It was the first of June, and the moors were beginning to bloom.

Elara knew the date the way she knew the hour of the dusk fire and the fold of every hollow for three hours in every direction — because she had been counting toward it all spring without ever calling it a plan. On the first of June, a year and a day since he had stepped backward into the void, she woke in the dead woman's bed at Blackmoor Hall and knew, with the quiet certainty of a thing that has finished turning, that today was the day.

She rose before the servants were moving. She did not take the satchel from the bottom of her trunk — the rope, the tinderbox, the brandy, her grandmother's pearls, the archaeology of the life that had ended on a cliff. She needed none of it. She needed only her stoutest boots and the faded gray-green ribbon on her wrist, worn thin as a whisper, and the road across the moors she had walked in her mind every day of the spring.

She dressed herself, which she had not done in more than a year: brown kirtle, stout boots, a shawl the color of the heather before it blooms. She braided her hair with her own fingers, and she looked at herself in the dead woman's glass and saw, for the first time in a year, not the mistress of Blackmoor Hall but the woman who had crossed the moors on foot and in terror and in love — thin, hollow-eyed, but there. Still there.

She left no note. She considered it, standing in the gray first light with her hand on the door. But a note would bring riders out to meet her on the road, and she did not want to be met. She wanted to walk alone, the way he had walked out of the world alone, and to stand where he had stood, and to have it be hers.

She went down the back stair, the one the servants used, because she had learned it the way she had learned the back stair at Thornwood — with her whole body, in the dark. The kitchen was not yet awake. She passed through the stillroom and out through the yard gate before the gate man had turned to his morning rounds, and then she was on the moor road, and the house was behind her, and she did not look back.

The walk was three hours. She had worked it out without meaning to, all spring, and now she walked it, and it was exactly as long as she had known it would be, and it was the strangest three hours of her life.

She walked fast at first, the way a woman walks who is afraid of being called back. The road climbed out of the valley past Blackmoor's last pastures and the drystone walls that marked the boundary of her husband's careful world, and then the walls fell away and the moors opened around her, and there was nothing but the sky and the heather and the wind and the sound of her own breath, and she slowed.

The heather was beginning to bloom — early still, a pale violet flush over the gray, like a promise. She had forgotten how the moors smelled in bloom, and she stopped on a crest and stood in it, and let herself be there.

She had not been on the moors since the flight. A year of east-tower windows had made her forget what they felt like under her feet. She walked the way Kael had taught her, reading the fold of the land without thinking: watching the bottoms, not the tops, where the light went in and did not come out, stepping stone to stone where the ground was bare. Her body remembered. That was the strange mercy of it. Her body had been taught by a man with gentle hands and a ruined back, and it carried her now across the gray country the way it had carried her then, when she had been running toward him instead of toward the place where he had gone.

She saw the sea before she saw the spur.

It came up over the last rise the way it had come up on the last day of the flight — gray and endless and alive, a whole horizon of it, breaking white on rocks she could not yet see. The wind off it hit her face, salt and cold, and she stopped, and for a long moment she could not breathe, because the last time she had seen that water, she had watched it close over him.

But it did not drown her. She stood on the rise with the sea before her and the wind moving in the heather, and she let it be the place where he had been nearest to her in all the world, and she did not turn away from it. The fear had loosened all spring, and what was left in her was not grief but something quieter, something that had a direction.

She walked on, down the last slope. Raven's Point stood out into the water the way she remembered it, a jagged tongue of rock over the black sea, and she climbed it the way they had climbed it, and then she was on the crown of it, and the world fell away on three sides, and there was nothing but the wind and the sky and the sea.

She stood where the riders had stood, feeling the shape of that day under her feet — the crescent of horses, her father at its head with his hands clasped behind his back, the patient iron of him. She walked forward slowly, the way a woman walks who is not afraid anymore, and came at last to the edge where the land gives up.

There was the ledge. She had not let herself picture it, all spring. She had let herself think of standing at the edge and breathing the salt air; she had not let herself picture the exact stone where he had pulled the ribbon from his wrist and thrown it to her and stepped backward into the void in silence. But now she was here, and she could not help it: she saw him. She saw the wind moving in his hair, his hands going to the ribbon, quick and certain, the way he had looked at her — not afraid, only sorry, only loving her — and she stood in the place where he had stood, and she did not weep.

She had been afraid, all spring, that she would weep. But the grief had spent itself differently. It had spent itself in east-tower afternoons and in the slow loosening of a woman letting go of everything, and what was left in her when she stood at the edge was not grief at all.

It was peace.

She stood at the edge of the rock, in the place where he had taken his final step, and looked down at the waves below — black and silver, heaving in long, unhurried swells, breaking white on the rocks. She had thought, in her darkest hours, that she would feel him here, that the place would be thick with him. But the place was not thick with him. It was empty, the way he had left it, the way he had chosen to leave it — and she understood, standing there with the wind in her face, that that was the whole of it.

He was not here. He was not in the water, waiting for her. He was not in the wind, calling her. He had gone into the sea, and the sea did not tell, the way she had told him it would not, and what was left of him in the world was not on this rock at all. What was left of him was in her. The one who knew. She had carried him for a year — through the wedding, through the dead woman's room, through the balanced ledgers and the cold nights and the east-tower window — and she had thought, all that time, that she was carrying him toward this place. But she understood now that she had been near him all along. He was not a place. He was the man who had taught her to read the fold of the land, the man who had promised her a door that stays, the man who had stepped backward into the void so that she could be the one who knew, and she had kept every word of it, and she had never once been far from him.

She did not jump.

That was the strange thing — the thing she had not known until she stood there. She had come to this place half-believing the current would take her. But she stood at the edge and looked down at the waves, and she did not want to go into them. The water was not him. The water had taken him, and she had hated it for a year, and standing above it she understood that it was only water — vast and gray and patient and alive, the thing he had wanted to see all his life and had seen for one terrible hour, the thing that had looked like her, and she had loved him for saying it.

She breathed the salt air, and she felt the strange peace of a thing that has finished. Not finished like an ending — finished like a long road walked to its end, like a fire burned down to coals that will hold warmth until morning. She stood there a long time, and the gulls turned above the water, and the heather bloomed behind her on the moors, and she was not weeping and she was not jumping, and she was not the mistress of Blackmoor Hall. She was the woman he had loved. She was his shore. She was the one who knew.

It was past noon when she finally moved. She did not want to leave; that was the truth of it. But the peace that had come to her on the edge was not the peace of staying. It was the peace of having come, of having stood where he stood, of having done what she had come to do — and the living belonged to her now, whether she wanted it or not.

She had promised him a fire at dusk.

The words came to her unbidden, in his voice, from a cold library in a house that existed now only in memory — a sailor wants somebody on shore to light a fire for him when he comes home. She had kept that promise by staying alive, by being the one who knows. She had kept it for a year. And standing at the edge of the rock, she understood that she would keep it one more day. That was all she had ever had to do — one more day, and then one more. She would walk back to Blackmoor Hall. She would light the fire at dusk. She would sit at the east-tower window and watch the moors, and she would be his shore, every dusk, forever, because the promise was the only thing left of her that was alive.

She turned away from the edge.

It was harder than standing there had been. Turning her back on the sea, on the place where he had gone, felt like the second leaving — worse than the first, because the first time she had been dragged. This time she walked. She walked away from the edge of the rock, down the shoulder of the spur, and she did not look back, because she knew if she looked back she might not be able to leave, and she had to leave. She had a fire to light.

The walk home was not the same walk. The same road, the same moors, the same heather — but not the same. Going out, she had walked toward something, with the current of the spring behind her. Going home, she walked with the peace in her, and she found that she was tired. Not the tiredness of the walk. A deeper tiredness — the tiredness of a woman who had been holding herself together with nothing but a promise and a ribbon for a year and a day, and who had finally, on a cliff above a black sea, laid the holding down.

She stopped once, on the crest of a rise, and looked back at the sea. The spur of Raven's Point stood out into it dark and small, and she looked at it a long moment, and she said his name aloud — Kael — the way she had not said it aloud in more than a year. She said it once, into the wind, and the wind took it, and she turned and walked on, and she did not need to say it again. She had been saying it all along.

She reached the gate of Blackmoor Hall in the long light of the early evening. The gate man let her in without a word. Mrs. Carrick met her at the door to the back stair, and Elara saw the housekeeper take her in — the boots, the hem of the kirtle dark with moor water, the hollows of her face — and Mrs. Carrick said nothing, only stood aside, and Elara passed her on the stair, and neither of them spoke.

She went up to the east tower and closed the door of the dead woman's room behind her. The room was as she had left it: the dust on the sill, the window looking out over the moors, the heather just beginning to bloom, the bed where she had lain for more than a year.

She stood at the window and looked out at the moors, and she saw the far gray smudge of the sea, and she knew the spur of Raven's Point stood somewhere out there in the falling light, empty of him, holding nothing, holding everything.

Then she crossed the room and lit the fire.

It was early for the fire — the house would not expect it for another hour — but she lit it anyway, with her own hands, the way she had promised him she would light it every dusk forever. She watched the flame catch and hold, and then she went to the bed, the dead woman's bed, and lay down on it, fully dressed, with her boots still on and the moor water still dark on her hem and the faded gray-green ribbon still around her wrist.

She did not rise again.

That was not a decision. It was not a surrender, and it was not the sea. It was simply that the walking was done. She had walked three hours out to the place where the land gives up, and she had stood at the edge and not jumped, and she had breathed the salt air and felt the strange peace, and she had walked three hours back, and she had lit the fire at dusk, and she had kept every promise she had ever made him except the one she could not keep — the one where they stood together at the edge of a heather garden watching the sea. She lay in the dead woman's bed with the fire burning in the hearth and the window showing the last gray light over the moors, and she closed her eyes, and she was his shore, and she was the one who knew, and she was very tired, and she let the tiredness have her.

Mrs. Carrick found her there the next morning, in the dead woman's room, with the fire burned down to coals and the lady still in her brown kirtle and her stout boots, her face turned toward the window, and the faded gray-green ribbon still on her wrist.

Still holding.

The housekeeper stood a long moment in the doorway. Then she crossed herself, the way her mother had taught her in the village, and she went down the back stair to the kitchen, and she told the cook, in a low voice, that the lady had gone to Raven's Point and come back, and that she thought the lady had finally stopped walking.

"What happened to her?" the cook asked.

"Nothing," Mrs. Carrick said. "Nothing at all. That's what happened."

The lady had walked to the edge of the world and had not jumped. She had stood where the land gives up and had not given up. She had come home and lit the fire at dusk, as she had promised, and then she had lain down, and the living had simply gone out of her, the way a fire goes out when there is nothing left to burn.

She had kept the promise to the very end. She had been his shore. She had been the one who knows.

And in the east tower of Blackmoor Hall, with the fire burned down to coals and the moors blooming violet in the first light of June, the woman who had promised a dead man a fire at dusk lay with her face turned toward the window, and she did not rise again, and the wind moved over the heather, and the sea took and took and took, remembering nothing, holding everything, the way she had held him.

set.name: Elara Ashworth
set.description: Now Lady Elara Vexford, 21, dark-haired, at Blackmoor Hall. On June 1 — the anniversary, a year and a day after Kael's leap — she woke at dawn, dressed herself for the first time in a year (brown kirtle, stout boots, shawl, hair braided by her own fingers), left no note, and walked alone the three hours from the gate of Blackmoor to Raven's Point, wearing the faded gray-green ribbon on her wrist. She stood at the edge where Kael took his final step, looked down at the black swells, did not jump, did not weep, and felt a strange peace: she understood he is not in the water but carried in her, the one who knows. She said his name aloud once into the wind on the way home, walked back in the long light of evening, passed Mrs. Carrick on the back stair without a word, lit the fire at dusk with her own hands (keeping her promise to be his shore), then lay down fully dressed in the dead first wife's bed and did not rise again. She left the satchel (rope, tinderbox, brandy, grandmother's pearls, silver pin, saved coin, Thornwood rear-door key) untouched at the bottom of her trunk. Condition: the walking is done; alive but the living has gone out of her — she will not rise again and will waste away through the winter into spring, still wearing the ribbon, her face turned to the window. Goal: keep Kael's memory and the fire at dusk to the end; reach the end she chose by walking out and coming back.

set.name: Lord Vexford
set.description: Lord Vexford, 49, widower, courteous, cold, pale colorless eyes, master of Blackmoor Hall, Elara's husband. He was away from the house — hunting or visiting neighbors, sleeping in Molly's rooms when at home — while his wife made her anniversary walk; he does not yet know she has taken to her bed. He remains almost content, baffled, uneasy, genuinely pleased with the household's management and genuinely restless; he thinks of his wife as a walking ghost and will not understand that she has stopped walking. Goal: the marriage and settlement undisturbed; maintain order and heirs in time. Condition: courteous and cold, absent much of the time; will return to find his wife bedridden and summon physicians in the months to come.

set.name: Mrs. Carrick
set.description: Mrs. Carrick, housekeeper of Blackmoor Hall, gray-haired, capable, twenty years in post. She saw the lady leave the yard at dawn on June 1 and noted her return in the long light of evening; she met her on the back stair and said nothing, only stood aside. The next morning she found the lady in the dead wife's room, still in kirtle and boots, the fire burned down to coals, face turned to the window, the faded gray-green ribbon still on her wrist; she crossed herself and told the cook, in a low voice, that the lady had gone to Raven's Point and come back and had finally stopped walking — 'Nothing at all. That's what happened.' She understands the lady kept her promise to the very end and will now see her through the coming winter, keeping the house running and the secret. Condition: grieving, quietly awed, keeping the lady's secret, frightened for what comes next.

On June 1, a year and a day after Kael's leap, Elara walked alone three hours from the gate of Blackmoor to Raven's Point, wearing the faded gray-green ribbon, dressed in brown kirtle and stout boots, leaving no note. She stood at the edge where Kael took his final step, looked down at the waves below, did not jump, did not weep, and felt a strange peace, understanding that Kael is not in the water but carried in her as the one who knows. She said his name aloud once into the wind on the way home.

After the anniversary walk, Elara returned to Blackmoor Hall in the long light of early evening, passed Mrs. Carrick on the back stair without a word, lit the fire at dusk with her own hands (keeping her promise), then lay down fully dressed in the dead first wife's bed with her boots on and the ribbon on her wrist, and did not rise again. Mrs. Carrick found her the next morning with the fire burned down to coals, her face turned to the window; she told the cook the lady had gone to Raven's Point and come back and had finally stopped walking. The satchel at the bottom of her trunk was left untouched.

Having lain down after the anniversary walk and not risen, Elara wastes away through the winter into the spring of her second year at Blackmoor; Lord Vexford summons physicians who can find no disease — she is simply leaving, her body following her spirit. In the spring, as the heather begins to bloom, she dies quietly in her sleep with her face turned toward the window (chapter 38).

They bury Elara in the Ashworth family plot at Thornwood, beside her father, Lord Aldous Ashworth, who died of apoplexy the previous winter — so Ashworth dies during the winter of Elara's second year at Blackmoor (chapter 38).

Elara's gravestone bears a single strange inscription written at her request: 'She walks the moors still.' The years pass and the story becomes a local legend: travelers crossing the moor sometimes glimpse a woman in gray walking toward Raven's Point (chapter 39).

chapters.name: The Heather Bloom
chapters.content:
The winter that followed the first of June was the longest winter in the memory of Blackmoor Hall.

It was not the cold. The cold came late and left early, and the moors wore only a light powdering of snow before the thaw set in. It was the stillness. From the day Mrs. Carrick found the lady in the dead woman's room with the fire burned down to coals, the house understood, without anyone saying it aloud, that something in the east tower had ended, and that the ending was not going to reverse itself.

Elara did not rise. That was the whole of it, and the whole of it held.

She lay in the dead wife's bed with her face turned toward the window, the way Mrs. Carrick had found her. She did not ask to be moved, and she did not ask to be washed, though she let the maids wash her when Mrs. Carrick insisted, and she let them take the boots off her feet at last. She ate what was put before her — a few spoonfuls of broth, a bite of bread — and then she stopped, and the trays went down again barely touched. She did not speak. She did not seem to be in pain. She lay with the faded gray-green ribbon still on her wrist, her eyes open in the mornings, closed at night, and every hour of the day she watched the window as though the moors were a book she was reading slowly and did not want to finish.

Mrs. Carrick came up every morning and every evening. She built the fire up at dusk herself now, because the lady could not, and because she believed the lady had lit that fire with her own hands for the last time on the first of June, and that the promise had been kept, and that no one had the right to ask more of her. She set the water and the clean linen, and she stood at the foot of the bed, and sometimes she spoke a few words about the house — the weather, the market, the new calf in the byre — and the lady listened, or did not listen, and it did not matter. What mattered was that the fire burned at dusk, and the window showed the moors, and the lady lay with her face turned toward them, still holding.

The physicians came because Lord Vexford summoned them.

He had not been at the house when his wife took to her bed. He had been at the port, or at Wrenfell, or somewhere the road turned — Mrs. Carrick never quite had the truth of it, and by the time word reached him and he rode home, the lady had been in the dead woman's room for a fortnight and the household had grown used to the quiet. Vexford stood in the doorway and looked at his wife, who did not turn her head to look at him, and he frowned, and he went downstairs and told the steward to send for a physician from the town.

The physician came. He was a small, precise man with spectacles and a bag of instruments, and he took the lady's wrist, and looked into her eyes, and listened to her heart, and asked her questions she did not answer. He bled her, because that was what physicians did, and she bore it without a sound, and he left a tonic on the nightstand that the maids poured down the washbasin when he was gone. He came again at the turn of the year, and again in the dead of winter, and each time he went down to the library where Vexford waited and told him the same thing: there was no disease. The pulse was weak but regular. The lungs were clear. The stomach was empty because the lady would not eat, and no tonic could fill a stomach that was not asked to hold.

"She is not ill, my lord," the physician said, folding his spectacles. "She is leaving. There is a difference, and it is not one medicine can cross."

Vexford paid him and did not send for him again.

He came to the room himself, now and then, because it was his house and his wife and he was a man who liked the accounts of things to balance. He stood at the foot of the bed in his black coat and looked at the hollow shell of the woman he had married, and he did not understand her, and he was honest enough to know it. He had never understood her. He had understood that she was beautiful and well-bred and that her father's lands marched with his, and he had understood that she ran the household flawlessly, and he had understood, in his way, that she was absent — that there was a door in her that had never opened to him. He had thought, when he took the red-haired kitchen maid to his rooms, that it did not matter. Now he stood in the dead woman's room — his first wife's room, kept exactly as it had been when she died — and looked at his second wife dying in it, and he thought, with a flicker of something that might have been unease if he had allowed it, that he had married the same death twice.

He said only one thing to her, standing at the foot of the bed. "You will not be buried here."

It was not a threat. It was, in its strange way, a concession — the nearest he could come to an apology. The Ashworths had their plot at Thornwood, and whatever else she was, Elara Vexford was an Ashworth, and the Ashworth plot was where she belonged, beside the father who had sold her and the mother who had wept. Vexford said the words and left, and Mrs. Carrick, who had heard them through the crack of the door, went down to the kitchen and told the cook that the lord had said the lady would not be buried here, and the cook crossed herself, and they did not speak of it again.

The winter closed in.

Mrs. Carrick kept the house running, because that was what she had done for twenty years and what she would do until they carried her out. She brought the lady broth and bread, and she built the fire at dusk, and she watched the ribbon on the lady's wrist grow thinner and grayer, and she told herself the lady was not waiting anymore — she was watching. There was a difference, and Mrs. Carrick, who had seen a great many people die, understood it.

The other servants kept their distance. The whisper that the lady was cursed had never quite died at Blackmoor Hall, and now it had proof: the mistress had walked to Raven's Point on the anniversary and come back and lain down, and she had not risen, and no physician could find a reason, because the reason was not in her body. The reason was in the moors, and the moors were what she watched, and the moors were what she was going toward, slowly, all winter long.

The red-haired kitchen maid, Molly, came to the door of the dead woman's room once, in the deep of the winter, when the lord was away and the house was quiet. She stood in the doorway in her silk wrapper and looked at the lady who was dying, and she did not know what she had come to say. She had heard the whispers that she would be the next lady, in time, and she had wanted to see what it looked like, the thing she was stepping toward.

Elara turned her head from the window, slowly, and looked at her.

It was the first time in months that she had looked at anyone, and Molly stood frozen in the doorway, and the two of them looked at each other across the length of the dead woman's room, and then Elara said, in a voice like the last coal of a fire, "He will not break you the way he broke her. He will only weary you. Do not let it weary you."

Molly did not understand. She stood a moment longer, then backed out of the room and went down to her rooms near the lord's chambers, and she did not come to the east tower again. She never told anyone what the lady had said, but she never forgot it either, and when she lay beside the lord at night and felt his cold courtesy close over her like water, she remembered the lady's voice, and she held onto something the lady had given her, though she could not have said what.

The winter wore on. The days shortened and lengthened. The moors froze and thawed and froze again, and Elara watched them from the window, and she grew thinner, and her dresses grew looser still, and Mrs. Carrick took them in, and the seamstress was not summoned, because the lady did not need to be fitted for anything anymore.

In the dead of the winter, word came to Blackmoor Hall of a death at Thornwood.

Lord Aldous Ashworth had died of apoplexy — so the letter said — in his study, in the middle of the afternoon, with the estate ledgers open before him and a fire burning in the grate. He had been found by Steward Hale, who had come in to ask about the spring sowing, and he had died the way he had lived: upright in his chair, silent, with his accounts balanced to the penny. The servants at Thornwood whispered, in the weeks that followed, that the old lord had been a changed man since the flight — that he had grown gray and quiet, that he had looked at the moors the way his daughter had once looked at them, that he had told the story of the groom who fled and the daughter who came home so many times that he had almost come to believe it.

The letter was brought to the library, and Vexford read it, and he did not trouble his wife with it. But Mrs. Carrick heard of it, because the servants always hear, and she stood a long time at the foot of the lady's bed, and she said, "Your father is dead, my lady. The apoplexy took him at Thornwood, in the winter."

Elara did not move. Her face was turned toward the window, and the window showed the moors, and the moors showed nothing.

Mrs. Carrick waited. Then she said, "They will bury him in the Ashworth plot."

And Elara said, very quietly, to the window, "Then there will be room beside him."

It was the most she had said in months, and Mrs. Carrick did not know what it meant, and she did not ask. She went down the back stair to the kitchen, and she told the cook that the lady had spoken, and the cook asked what she had said, and Mrs. Carrick said she had said there would be room beside her father in the Ashworth plot, and the cook crossed herself, and neither of them said anything more.

The winter ended the way winters end — not all at once, but by increments, by the lengthening of the light. Elara watched it from the window: the retreat of the frost, the first softness of the ground, the water running in the hollows. She did not rally with the spring, the way the household hoped she might. She lay in the dead woman's bed and watched the moors turn from gray to a gray faintly touched with green, and she grew thinner still, and the ribbon on her wrist grew grayer still, and Mrs. Carrick fed her broth and built the fire at dusk and watched her go.

In the last week of April, the heather began to bloom.

It came early that year, the way it had come early the year before — a pale violet flush spreading over the gray, like a promise kept. Elara watched it deepen from a flush to a wash to a tide of color rolling down the slopes toward the sea, and she watched it the way she had watched it on the first of June, walking out across the moors to the place where the land gives up. She had walked through the heather in bloom to stand at the edge of the world, and she had not jumped, and she had come home and lit the fire at dusk, and she had lain down. And now the heather was blooming again, and the walking was done, and the keeping was done, and there was nothing left but the watching.

On the last evening of April, Mrs. Carrick came up to the east tower as she always did, and she found the lady with her face turned toward the window, and the window showed the moors blooming violet in the long light, and the lady's eyes were open and quiet, and her breath was very light.

Mrs. Carrick built the fire. She set the water. She stood at the foot of the bed, and she said, "The heather is out early this year, my lady."

And Elara said, without turning her head, "He would have liked that."

It was the last thing she said. Mrs. Carrick stood a long moment, then went down the back stair, because there was nothing else to do, and the fire burned in the hearth, and the window showed the moors, and the heather bloomed.

Elara died in her sleep that night, with the fire burning and the window open on the dark and the moors blooming violet beyond it, her face turned toward the moors, the faded gray-green ribbon still on her wrist.

It was not a decision. It was not a surrender. It was simply that the watching was done, the way the walking had been done, the way the keeping had been done — one thing after another, laid down, until there was nothing left to lay down but the woman herself, and she lay down too, and the living went out of her the way a fire goes out when there is nothing left to burn. She had kept the promise. She had lit the fire at dusk, and the fire had held, and she had been his shore, and she had been the one who knows, and she was very tired, and the heather was blooming, and she let go.

Mrs. Carrick found her in the morning, and she stood a long time at the foot of the bed, and then she crossed herself, and she went down to tell the lord.

They buried her in the Ashworth family plot at Thornwood, as Vexford had said, beside her father, who had died of apoplexy the previous winter.

The journey was a gray, quiet procession: the coffin on the cart, the black horses, the servants of Blackmoor Hall walking behind, the moors blooming violet on either side of the road. At Thornwood they received her like a stranger, because that was what she had become. Lady Margaret Ashworth, gray and shrunken in her widow's black, stood at the grave with her hands folded and did not weep, because she had wept all her tears over her daughter years ago and had none left. Martha stood at the edge of the gathering with her weigher's eyes and watched the coffin lowered, and she did not know what she felt, and she did not let it show. Pip, the stable boy, grown taller and quieter, stood with his cap crushed in his fists, and he thought of the knotted cloth of coin still under his shirt, and the man who had taught him to curry a horse, and the lady who had looked at him once in the harness room and said nothing, and he did not know where the money belonged now, and he held it anyway.

They lowered the coffin into the earth beside Lord Aldous Ashworth, and the earth closed over her, and the mourners dispersed, and the heather bloomed on the moors around the plot, and the wind moved over it, and the sea took and took and took in the far distance, remembering nothing.

At Blackmoor Hall, Mrs. Carrick went up to the east tower the day after the burial, because it had to be done, and she stood in the dead woman's room — her first mistress's room, and then her second — and she looked at the empty bed with the sheets stripped, and the window showing the moors, and the fire burned down to ash in the grate.

And she opened the window, the way she had never done while the lady was alive, and she let the spring air in.

The wind came off the moors, and it smelled of heather, and it moved through the empty room, and Mrs. Carrick stood there a long moment, and then she closed the window, and she went down the back stair, and the house settled into its new quiet, and the heather bloomed, and the moors endured, holding the memory of everything, the way the lady had held him.

set.name: Elara Ashworth
set.description: Dead. Lady Elara Vexford wasted away through the winter into spring and died quietly in her sleep on the last night of April in the dead first wife's room at Blackmoor Hall, with the fire Mrs. Carrick had built burning down, the window open on the dark, her face turned toward the moors blooming violet, and the faded gray-green ribbon still on her wrist. Her last words, to Mrs. Carrick about the early heather, were 'He would have liked that.' Earlier that winter she told Molly once, from her bed, 'He will not break you the way he broke her. He will only weary you. Do not let it weary you.' She was buried in the Ashworth family plot at Thornwood beside her father, Lord Aldous Ashworth, who died of apoplexy the previous winter; Vexford conceded she would not be buried at Blackmoor. She kept her promise to the very end: fire at dusk, his shore, the one who knows. Goal: accomplished — she reached the end she chose by walking out and coming back; she is at rest beside her father, the heather blooming over her.

set.name: Lady Margaret Ashworth
set.description: Lady Margaret Ashworth, widow of Lord Aldous Ashworth (he died of apoplexy the previous winter), gray and shrunken in her widow's black, at Thornwood. She stood at her daughter's grave with folded hands and did not weep — she wept all her tears years ago. She lost the husband she married for land and the daughter she pushed into the Vexford match; she is hollowed out, keeping up appearances at Thornwood, the world she schemed for now empty around her.

set.name: Lord Aldous Ashworth
set.description: Dead. Lord Aldous Ashworth died of apoplexy in his study at Thornwood in the dead of winter (Elara's second winter at Blackmoor), in the middle of the afternoon, with the estate ledgers open before him and a fire burning, found by Steward Hale. The servants whispered he was a changed man since the flight — gray and quiet, staring at the moors — and that he told the cleaning story (the groom fled, the daughter came home) so many times he almost believed it. He erased Kael from the world's record and kept the Vexford settlement intact; his daughter is buried beside him in the Ashworth plot.

set.name: Martha
set.description: Martha, sour-faced, efficient lady's maid, about thirty, at Thornwood in the household of the widowed Lady Margaret. She stood at the edge of Elara's burial with her weigher's eyes and watched the coffin lowered, and she does not know what she feels, and she does not let it show. Her secret — that she delivered the lovers to Ashworth — is still kept; she keeps her place, watchful and exposed enough to fear, waiting to see what the diminished household brings.

set.name: Lord Vexford
set.description: Lord Vexford, widower twice over now, 51, courteous, cold, pale colorless eyes, master of Blackmoor Hall. He summoned physicians for his wasting wife and was told there was no disease — 'She is leaving' — and paid them and did not send again. He stood once at the foot of her bed and said 'You will not be buried here,' the nearest he could come to a concession, and kept his word: Elara was buried in the Ashworth plot at Thornwood. He is uneasy at having married the same death twice (his first wife's room kept as she left it, his second wife dying in it), keeps his mistress Molly in her rooms near his chambers, and will now have to decide whether to marry again. Goal: the settlement undisturbed; an heir in time — still unfulfilled. Condition: courteous, cold, absent much of the time, the house quieter than ever.

set.name: Pip
set.description: Pip, stable boy at Thornwood, grown taller and quieter in the years since the flight, grieving. He stood at Elara's grave with his cap crushed in his fists, thinking of the knotted cloth of coin still under his shirt — Kael's hidden savings — and of the man who taught him to curry a horse and the lady who once looked at him in the harness room and said nothing. He does not know where the money belongs now that both of them are gone, and he holds it anyway, telling no one. Goal: survive; keep the cloth safe.

set.name: Mrs. Carrick
set.description: Mrs. Carrick, housekeeper of Blackmoor Hall, gray-haired, capable, twenty-plus years in post, grieving and quietly awed. She tended Elara through the whole decline — built the fire at dusk every night herself, fed her broth, watched the ribbon grow grayer, heard Vexford say the lady would not be buried here, and carried the news of Lord Ashworth's death to her ('Then there will be room beside him').
