She was with her at the last, heard her final words about the heather, found her dead in the morning, and saw her buried from Thornwood. The day after the burial she opened the east-tower window for the first time and let the spring air in. She keeps the lady's secret and her memory, and the house settles into its new quiet under her hand.

set.name: Molly
set.description: Molly, the red-haired kitchen maid turned Lord Vexford's mistress, about Elara's age, a face like a milkmaid in a song and eyes that want things, still at Blackmoor Hall in the silk wrapper and the room near the lord's chambers. In the deep winter she once came to the door of the dying lady's room, and Elara told her: 'He will not break you the way he broke her. He will only weary you. Do not let it weary you.' Molly did not understand then, backed out, never told anyone, and never forgot; she holds onto the lady's words when Vexford's cold courtesy closes over her, and the servants now whisper she will be the next lady in time. Goal: keep the lord's favor, rise in the house, survive. Condition: young, hopeful, frightened, alive, carrying a gift she cannot name.

After the first-of-June anniversary walk and her lying down, Elara wasted away through the winter into spring at Blackmoor Hall: she never rose, let the maids wash her, ate only spoonfuls of broth and bread, did not speak except twice, watched the moors from the dead wife's bed with the faded gray-green ribbon on her wrist while Mrs. Carrick built the fire at dusk. She died quietly in her sleep on the last night of April as the heather bloomed early.

Lord Vexford summoned a physician from the town, who bled Elara, found no disease, left a tonic the maids poured away, and returned at the turn of the year and in deep winter, telling Vexford each time: 'She is not ill. She is leaving. There is a difference, and it is not one medicine can cross.' Vexford paid him and did not send for him again.

Standing at the foot of the dying lady's bed, Lord Vexford said only 'You will not be buried here' — in its strange way a concession, sending her back to the Ashworth plot at Thornwood. Mrs. Carrick heard it through the crack of the door and told the cook; the lord kept his word.

In the deep of winter, the red-haired kitchen maid Molly came once to the door of the dead woman's room in her silk wrapper, wanting to see the lady she was rumored to replace. Elara turned her head, the first time in months she had looked at anyone, and said: 'He will not break you the way he broke her. He will only weary you. Do not let it weary you.' Molly backed out, never understood it, never told anyone, and never forgot it.

Word reached Blackmoor in the dead of winter that Lord Aldous Ashworth had died of apoplexy in his study at Thornwood, mid-afternoon, ledgers open, fire burning, found by Steward Hale. The Thornwood servants whispered he was a changed man since the flight — gray and quiet, staring at the moors — and that he told the cleaning story (the groom fled, the daughter came home) so many times he almost believed it. Elara's only words on hearing it: 'Then there will be room beside him.'

Elara was buried in the Ashworth family plot at Thornwood beside her father, Lord Aldous Ashworth, in a gray quiet procession of black horses and Blackmoor servants through the blooming heather. Margaret stood gray and shrunken in widow's black with no tears left; Martha watched with weigher's eyes; Pip held the knotted cloth of coin under his shirt and did not know where it belonged now. The earth closed over her and the heather bloomed on the moors around the plot. The day after, Mrs. Carrick opened the east-tower window for the first time and let the spring air in.

Pip still carries Kael's knotted cloth of coin under his shirt at Thornwood; with both Kael and Elara dead and buried, he does not know where the money belongs now. Its fate may surface in the epilogue (chapter 39) as part of how the story is remembered.

chapters.name: The Moors Still Walk Her
chapters.content:
The stone stands at the edge of the Ashworth plot, beneath the hawthorn where the heather comes in first. It is not a grand stone. Lord Aldous Ashworth lies under a slab carved with his name and dates and the full weight of his offices; his daughter's is a narrow upright stone, pale as a bone, and when the stonecutter from Merrow set it into the spring earth he thought the words he had been given must be a mistake.

SHE WALKS THE MOORS STILL.

The words were delivered to him on a slip of paper in Lady Margaret's own hand, and beneath them, smaller, the name and the dates: ELARA ASHWORTH VEXFORD. The stonecutter asked, twice, if the lady of Thornwood was certain, for no one had ever asked such a thing of him, and Margaret, gray and shrunken in her widow's black, told him yes, that the words had been her daughter's own last request, carried out of Blackmoor Hall by the housekeeper's mouth and set down in writing at the dying woman's bedside.

"He said you would want to know," Mrs. Carrick had told Margaret at the burial, when the earth was still raw and the smell of turned clay lay on the air. "She said it twice, near the end. She said, 'Write on my stone: she walks the moors still.' And then she said —" Mrs. Carrick's voice had gone thin as thread. "She said, 'He will know where to find me.'"

Margaret had not asked who "he" was. She had stopped asking questions years before, the way a woman stops opening windows in a house that has grown too cold. She only nodded, folded her hands over the black of her dress, and ordered the stone.

The first year, Margaret tended the plot herself. She pulled the weeds, set the small stones upright again after the frost heaved them, and planted early heather where the grass would not take. It gave her hands something to do and her heart something to refuse to feel. She was sixty-two and looked eighty; the woman who had schemed for a titled son-in-law now had a title in the family — Lady Vexford her daughter had been, for four years and a season — and the house was emptier than it had ever been. Thornwood held perhaps half its old staff now. The young ones had gone off to the towns or the wars; the old ones stayed because there was nowhere else to go.

Martha stayed. That was the strangest thing, to Margaret's mind: the sour-faced maid who had watched everything for twenty years stayed on, efficient as ever, keeping the diminished household running under a weigher's eye. Margaret sometimes caught Martha standing at the long hall window at dusk, looking out at the moors, and wondered what she was weighing. She never asked. There were many things in that house that were not asked about.

What Margaret did not know was that Martha went out before first light, twice a month through all the years, and weeded the narrow stone herself — that the plot Margaret tended by day was kept trim by another pair of hands before the household stirred. Martha never said a word about it, and she never knew what she felt when she knelt in the dew with her fingers in the dark earth: not grief, not guilt, nothing so clean. She had carried a secret like a blade for the better part of a lifetime, had delivered two lovers into the hands of a man who broke them, and the blade had never once been drawn on her. That was the whole of it, she told herself. She had kept her place. And yet she came back to the stone, twice a month, and pulled the weeds, and did not let it show.

Bess was the one who went. In the spring after the burial, Bess, round-faced and quick, gave notice and married a carter from Merrow who hauled wool for her uncle's merchant. On her last evening at Thornwood she walked out to the Ashworth plot alone and stood at the narrow stone a long time in the falling light. She had helped a lady out of a locked room once, had hidden a cloak and a satchel and two loaves of bread behind the pickle jars, and she had never known, not truly, what became of the lady after the gray dawn when the riders went east and came back with Lord Ashworth and the gray horse and no bride in the white gown. She knew now, of course; everyone knew the shape of it — the wedding four days later, the years at Blackmoor, the wasting. What Bess carried out of that graveyard was not guilt. It was a kind of reverence. She had given a woman three days of freedom and a road to the sea, and whatever came after, she believed the lady had died knowing she had been loved, and that was more than most people ever got.

Bess told the story once, years later, to her own children in the kitchen of the house in Merrow — not the whole of it, never the names, but the shape: a lady in a tower, a man in the stable, a door left unlocked. "She was the bravest person I ever knew," Bess said, and her children thought it was a fairy tale.

It became one, in time.

The legend did not start at the grave. It started, as such things do, with a traveler. Two years after the burial, a peddler crossing the eastern moors at dusk — the same sort of peddler, some said, who had once told a lady in a brown kirtle where to find her man — stopped at the herder's bothy above the Merrow road and swore he had seen a woman walking the high path toward Raven's Point: a woman in gray, her face turned toward the sea, and when he called out to her she did not turn, and when he reached the place where she had been there was no one, only the heather moving in the wind.

The herder laughed and gave him a bowl of stew. "That'll be the Ashworth lady," he said. "She walks the moors still."

The words on the stone had done their work. They spread the way seed spreads, by wind and bird and the boots of men. Within a year every shepherd between Thornwood and the coast had a version. Some said the woman in gray was looking for a man who fell from the cliffs. Some said she was waiting for a door that stays. The old men, the ones who remembered, said nothing at all and touched their caps when they passed the narrow stone, because they had known a stable hand once who calmed a mad stallion with his bare hands and who had vanished one dawn with the lash still wet on his back, and they had known the lady who stopped eating, and they did not need a ghost to explain the wind.

But the seeing went on. That was the strange part. It was not grief and it was not invention — or if it was, it wore the body of weather. Travelers crossing the moor in the long light of June, when the heather comes in violet and the air smells of salt and honey, would look up the slope toward Raven's Point and see a figure in gray, small against the sky, walking steadily, unhurried, her face turned toward the sea. She was seen in mist and in full sun. A drover coming up from the coast with a string of cattle, who had never heard the story, reported a woman on the cliff path who waved once, slowly, as if blessing the road, and then was gone where no path was. A pair of young lovers eloping north to the hidden villages saw her on the high moor above the sea, took her for a sign, and were married at the little chapel at Crowse; they lived to be old and told their grandchildren that the lady of the moors had watched them pass. A soldier returning from the wars, walking home by night with his discharge papers in his boot, saw a lantern of light in the mist above the cliff and heard, or thought he heard, a woman singing — not a song, just a sound, the way the sea sings — and it carried him the last mile to his mother's door.

The Thornwood servants told the travelers the tale when they stopped for bread and a fire, and the tale grew with the telling. The lady had been beautiful. The lady had been cursed. The lady had loved a man beneath her and the world had broken them both. Some versions put the man in the ground and the lady in the sea; some had it the other way round. Only the ending stayed the same in every telling, because the stone said so: she walks the moors still. And the land itself seemed to agree. The moors had always been a place that kept things — the fold of a hollow that had hidden a fleeing woman and a wanted man, the deep places where the light went in and did not come out — and it kept the lady the way it kept the memory of rain, in the color of the heather and the sound of the wind.

Pip knew the true version. Pip was no longer a stable boy; he was head groom at Thornwood now, a quiet man of thirty with a face that had forgotten how to laugh and hands that had learned to be gentle with frightened horses, because a man had taught him once, in the loft above the tack room, that a horse is only afraid and it is your job to be the thing it is not afraid of. Pip kept the knotted cloth. He had kept it for years, through two masters and the long quiet, through the winter Lord Ashworth died and the spring the lady came home in a coffin. It had grown soft with the sweat of his life, the coins inside worn thin from being held. He had never spent a penny of it. He did not know, still, where it belonged. He kept the old gray gelding, too, in the home paddock where the grass was sweet, and refused to sell him though the horse was ancient now, because the gelding had carried the lady on the longest road of her life and Pip would not be the one to end it.

Then one dusk in the seventh summer, Pip walked out to the Ashworth plot alone — he did this every year on the same evening, the evening before the first of June, though he could not have said why — and stood at the narrow stone, and understood. The lady had once looked at him in the harness room and said nothing at all, and he had known she knew about the cloth, and her silence had been the kindest thing anyone in that house had ever done for him. Kael had hidden the coin to buy a cart and a mule and a road to the sea for the two of them. The lady had carried the dream to the cliff's edge and beyond. Pip knelt in the heather, worked his knife under the sod at the foot of the stone, and buried the knotted cloth deep, in the good dark earth where the roots of the heather would find it and hold it. "There," he said, to no one, in a voice rough with years. "Now it's where it belongs. It bought you your road."

He never told anyone. But from that summer the heather at the foot of the narrow stone came in thicker and darker than anywhere else in the plot, a blaze of violet at the edge of the green, and the servants said it was the lady's own doing, and the travelers who saw it took it for a sign.

At Blackmoor Hall the years settled differently. Lord Vexford, courteous and cold, had not remarried. He had considered it — there had been negotiations, twice, with families who wanted a title and a wide estate and did not ask too closely how two wives had died in the same room — but something in him balked, and he spent more and more of his time away, hunting with the Earl of Barrow, visiting the port, letting the estate run itself under the steward and the housekeeper. Molly had not become the next lady. She had stayed in her rooms near his chambers, growing from a girl with a face like a milkmaid in a song into a woman with the same wanting eyes and a thicker skin, and she had never told anyone what the dying lady had said to her in the deep of the winter, but she had kept it, the way she kept everything now, close and careful. "He will not break you the way he broke her. He will only weary you. Do not let it weary you." Molly had not let it weary her. She had learned the ledgers, the way the lady had, and the house ran smooth under her hand, and when the servants whispered that she ought to be the lady in truth, Molly said nothing at all.

It was Mrs. Carrick who kept the real memory. Mrs. Carrick, gray-haired and capable, past sixty now, still housekeeper of Blackmoor Hall, had opened the east-tower window the day after the burial and let the spring air in, and she had never closed it since. The dead first wife's room — the room where two women had lain down and not risen — was aired now, swept now, the dust gone, the bed made fresh, though no one slept in it. Mrs. Carrick did that herself every morning with her own hands, and if anyone asked she said it was respect. She told the story once, to a new maid who asked why the window was always open and who the gray lady was, and she told it plain and true, the way it had happened, without ghosts and without embellishment, and the maid wept, and Mrs. Carrick said, "There now. She'd not want tears. She'd want you to light the fire at dusk and mean it."

On the high moor above the sea, on a June evening in the year the heather came in early, a young shepherd — the grandson of the herder who had fed the peddler — drove his flock down the long slope toward the fold and saw, on the path to Raven's Point, a woman in gray. She was far off, no more than a shape against the falling light, walking steadily with her face turned toward the sea, and the sheep paid her no mind, and the wind blew, and when the shepherd looked again she was gone, and there was only the heather, violet to the edge of the cliff, and the sound of the sea below.

He was not afraid. His grandfather had told him the story. He stood a long time watching the empty path, and then he touched his cap to the place where she had been, the way the old men did, and went down to the bothy and lit the fire for the night.

And the moors endured. That is the last thing, and the truest. Thornwood stands, cold and silent, its upper windows dark where the rooms are shut up, a monument to the world that broke her, and it will stand until the stone crumbles and the name wears away. But the moors do not care for monuments. They go on. The wind goes on, and it carries the sound of two names if you know how to listen. The heather goes on, blooming every June over the narrow stone and over the fold where a man and a woman once lay hidden while the riders passed within yards, unseen. The sea goes on, breaking below Raven's Point, where the land gives up and the memory of a man who stepped backward into the void comes home on every tide. The moors hold them both, the lady and the man, the way they hold every secret ever entrusted to them, and they give it back in the only way they can: in the color of the heather, and the sound of the wind, and the figure of a woman in gray, walking toward the sea, walking the moors still.

set.name: Elara Ashworth
set.description: Dead, buried in the Ashworth family plot at Thornwood beside her father. Her narrow pale stone bears the inscription she requested: 'SHE WALKS THE MOORS STILL' with her name and dates beneath, carved from a slip of paper Margaret sent to the stonecutter at Merrow (words carried from Blackmoor by Mrs. Carrick, who heard Elara say them twice near the end, adding 'He will know where to find me'). She is at rest, and her memory has become a local legend: the woman in gray seen by travelers on the high moor walking toward Raven's Point with her face turned to the sea. The moors hold her memory and Kael's; the heather blooms thicker and darker at the foot of her stone since Pip buried Kael's coin there.

set.name: Lady Margaret Ashworth
set.description: Gray, shrunken, sixty-two (looking eighty), widow of Lord Aldous Ashworth, at Thornwood in her widow's black, keeping the diminished household (about half its old staff) running. She ordered the narrow gravestone with her daughter's strange inscription from the stonecutter at Merrow, asking twice whether it was meant; she tended the Ashworth plot herself the first year, planting early heather, giving her hands something to do and her heart something to refuse to feel. She does not ask who 'he' was and never asks about the many things in the house that are not spoken of. She is hollowed out, keeping up appearances.

set.name: Lord Aldous Ashworth
set.description: Dead, buried under a slab with his name, dates, and offices at the head of the Ashworth plot at Thornwood, beside his daughter Elara. He died of apoplexy in his study the previous winter. The servants whispered he was a changed man since the flight, telling the cleaning story so many times he almost believed it. His daughter's narrow stone stands at the edge of the plot beneath the hawthorn, near but apart from his.

set.name: Martha
set.description: Still at Thornwood in the household of the widowed Lady Margaret, about fifty, sour-faced, efficient, the longest-serving maid, keeping the diminished household running under her weigher's eye. Her secret — that she delivered the lovers to Ashworth — is still kept and still unpunished. Twice a month before first light, through all the years, she goes out and secretly weeds Elara's grave herself, never telling anyone, never knowing what she feels — not grief, not guilt, something less clean; she keeps her place, watchful and exposed enough to fear.

set.name: Lord Vexford
set.description: Lord Vexford, widower twice over, in his late fifties, courteous, cold, pale colorless eyes, master of Blackmoor Hall. He did not remarry; he considered negotiations twice with families who wanted a title and wide estate and did not ask how two wives died in the same room, but balked both times. He spends more and more time away hunting with the Earl of Barrow or visiting the port, letting the estate run under the steward and Mrs. Carrick. The dead first wife's room — where two wives lay down and did not rise — is now aired and swept daily by Mrs. Carrick, though no one sleeps in it. Condition: absent much of the time, courteous, cold, the house quieter than ever; no heir.

set.name: Kael
set.description: Kael, stable hand turned fugitive, dead. He stepped backward into the void at Raven's Point and the black sea swallowed him; no grave, no marker, no name. He lives on in legend and memory: the fishermen of the coast remember the moorman the sea took; the legend of the woman in gray walking toward Raven's Point is bound to the story of the man she loved; and the sea breaking below the Point brings his memory home on every tide. The moors hold his memory and Elara's together.

set.name: Steward Hale
set.description: Steward Hale, gray-faced, folded hands, a tool who chose to remain a tool, at Thornwood. He rode in the pursuit, stood in the crescent at Raven's Point, and returned with the riders; he served Lord Ashworth, now dead, and continues to serve the diminished household under Lady Margaret. Goal: serve the house. Condition: obedient, silent.

set.name: Pip
set.description: Now head groom at Thornwood, about thirty, a quiet man whose face forgot how to laugh and whose hands learned gentleness with frightened horses from a man in the loft above the tack room. He kept Kael's knotted cloth of coin for years through two masters and the long quiet, never spending a penny of it, not knowing where it belonged; on the seventh summer, at dusk on the eve of the first of June, he knelt at Elara's stone and buried the knotted cloth deep in the earth at its foot, saying 'Now it's where it belongs. It bought you your road.' He also kept the ancient gray gelding Storm in the home paddock and refuses to sell him. He walks to the Ashworth plot alone every year on the evening before the first of June.

set.name: Bess
set.description: Bess, the young kitchen maid who aided Elara's flight, gave notice in the spring after Elara's burial and married a carter from Merrow who hauls wool for her uncle's merchant. On her last evening at Thornwood she stood alone at the narrow stone in the falling light, carrying not guilt but a kind of reverence — she had given a woman three days of freedom and a road to the sea. Years later she told her own children the story without names, as a fairy tale of a lady in a tower, a man in a stable, and a door left unlocked, saying 'She was the bravest person I ever knew.' Goal: live her life in Merrow. Condition: content, loyal to the memory.

set.name: Storm
set.description: Storm, the gray gelding, now ancient, kept in the home paddock at Thornwood where the grass is sweet, tended by Pip, who refuses to sell him. He carried Elara and Kael for six days of flight and stood with them at the end at Raven's Point, and was led home by Bren. He is old, sound, and cared for, the last living creature of the flight besides Pip's memory.

set.name: Mrs. Carrick
set.description: Mrs. Carrick, housekeeper of Blackmoor Hall, gray-haired, capable, past sixty, twenty-plus years in post, still in service. She carried Elara's last words out of Blackmoor to Margaret at the burial ('Write on my stone: she walks the moors still' and 'He will know where to find me'). She opened the east-tower window the day after the burial and has never closed it since; she airs and sweeps the dead first wife's room herself every morning, calling it respect. She tells the story plain and true, without ghosts, to any maid who asks, and ends it: 'She'd not want tears. She'd want you to light the fire at dusk and mean it.' Goal: keep the lady's memory and the house. Condition: grieving, quietly awed, steady.

set.name: Molly
set.description: Molly, the red-haired kitchen maid turned Lord Vexford's mistress, now a woman in her early thirties with the same wanting eyes and a thicker skin, still at Blackmoor Hall in her rooms near the lord's chambers. She did not become the next lady; Vexford never remarried. She kept the dying Elara's words — 'He will not break you the way he broke her. He will only weary you. Do not let it weary you.' — close and careful, never telling anyone, and did not let it weary her: she learned the ledgers the way the lady had, and the house runs smooth under her hand and Mrs. Carrick's. When servants whisper she ought to be the lady in truth, she says nothing. Goal: keep the lord's favor, survive, keep the house. Condition: young at heart, hopeful, frightened, alive, carrying a gift she cannot name.

Elara's narrow gravestone in the Ashworth plot at Thornwood bears the inscription written at her request, 'She walks the moors still,' with ELARA ASHWORTH VEXFORD and her dates beneath. Margaret sent the words on a slip of paper to the stonecutter at Merrow, who asked twice if it was meant; the words were carried from Blackmoor by Mrs. Carrick, who heard Elara say them twice near the end and add 'He will know where to find me.'

For years after the burial, Martha, without telling anyone and without understanding what she feels, goes out before first light twice a month and secretly weeds Elara's grave herself, keeping the plot trim before the household stirs. Her secret about the betrayal remains kept and unpunished.

In the spring after Elara's burial, Bess gave notice at Thornwood and married a carter from Merrow who hauls wool for her uncle's merchant; on her last evening she stood alone at the narrow stone. Years later she told her children the story without names as a fairy tale of a lady in a tower, a man in a stable, and a door left unlocked, saying 'She was the bravest person I ever knew.'

In the seventh summer, on the eve of the first of June, Pip (now head groom at Thornwood) knelt at Elara's stone and buried Kael's knotted cloth of coin, which he had carried unspent for years, deep in the earth at the foot of the stone, saying 'Now it's where it belongs. It bought you your road.' From that summer the heather at the foot of the narrow stone came in thicker and darker than anywhere else in the plot.

The legend of the woman in gray began about two years after the burial, when a peddler crossing the eastern moors at dusk swore he saw a woman in gray walking the high path toward Raven's Point with her face turned to the sea, and found no one where she had been. The words on the stone spread the tale; within a year every shepherd between Thornwood and the coast had a version, and the seeings continued for years — travelers, drovers, eloping lovers, and a returning soldier all reported the gray figure walking toward the sea, and the eloping pair were married at Crowse and lived to be old, telling their grandchildren the lady of the moors watched them pass.

Lord Vexford did not marry again, though he twice entered negotiations with families who wanted a title and a wide estate and did not ask how two wives died in the same room; both times he balked. He spends more and more time away hunting or at the port, and the estate runs under the steward and Mrs. Carrick, with Molly, who learned the ledgers the way Elara had, steadying the house.

Mrs. Carrick opened the east-tower window of the dead first wife's room the day after Elara's burial and never closed it since; she airs and sweeps the room herself every morning as an act of respect, and tells the lady's story plain and true to any maid who asks, ending it: 'She'd not want tears. She'd want you to light the fire at dusk and mean it.'

errors.quote: On the first of June, a year and a day since he had stepped backward into the void, she woke in the dead woman's bed at Blackmoor Hall and knew, with the quiet certainty of a thing that has finished turning, that today was the day.
errors.location: Chapter 37, paragraph beginning 'It was the first of June'
errors.pair: "We go," he said. "The night before midsummer. We go together, and we don't look back."

errors.quote: In the last week of April, the heather began to bloom. It came early that year, the way it had come early the year before — a pale violet flush spreading over the gray, like a promise kept.
errors.location: Chapter 38, paragraph beginning 'In the last week of April'
errors.pair: The heather was beginning to bloom — early still, a pale violet flush over the gray, like a promise.
errors.pair_location: Chapter 37, paragraph beginning 'The heather was beginning to bloom'

errors.quote: It was Mrs. Carrick who kept the real memory. Mrs. Carrick, gray-haired and capable, past sixty now, still housekeeper of Blackmoor Hall, had opened the east-tower window the day after the burial and let the spring air in, and she had never closed it since.
errors.location: Chapter 39, paragraph beginning 'It was Mrs. Carrick who kept the real memory'
errors.pair: Mrs. Carrick stood there a long moment, and then she closed the window, and she went down the back stair, and the house settled into its new quiet, and the heather bloomed, and the moors endured, holding the memory of everything, the way the lady had held him.
errors.element: physical state of the east-tower window

errors.quote: The walk was three hours. She had worked it out without meaning to, all spring, and now she walked it, and it was exactly as long as she had known it would be, and it was the strangest three hours of her life.
errors.location: Chapter 37, paragraph beginning 'The walk was three hours'
